articles.title_orig: China, Canada expand tariff relief after Carney-Xi meeting
articles.title_zh: China, Canada expand tariff relief after Carney-Xi meeting
articles.content_orig:
Canada and China have agreed to cut tariffs on more goods, as Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney continues to look to decrease his country’s dependence on the United States amid President Donald Trump’s tariffs.
Meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen on Tuesday, Carney and Chinese President Xi Jinping announced new tariff remissions, building on an agreement they made in January to open up trade and start to repair a strained diplomatic relationship.
China will offer tariff relief on about 400 million Canadian dollars ($280m) worth of Canadian exports, including frozen pork and seafood, said a statement from Carney’s office.
Canada, in exchange, will keep tariff exemptions for certain Chinese steel and aluminium products in place for another two years, and add remissions to another 32 steel and aluminium items that Canada doesn’t have enough of.
Xi said stronger ties served both countries’ interests and supported global stability and prosperity.
“This is the right choice,” he said.
Carney praised the greater predictability in the relationship and said Canada was ahead of schedule on its goal of increasing exports to China by 50 percent by the end of the decade.
Under the January agreement, Canada lowered its 100 percent tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1 percent, allowing an initial 49,000 vehicles into the country each year. That cap is set to rise to 70,000 over five years.
In return, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products and recently extended relief for canola meal, peas, lobster and crab for another two years.
The deal comes a day after Carney said Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if talks with Washington fail to hold together the closely integrated North American auto industry.
“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia on Monday. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions.”
The comments prompted a backlash from White House trade adviser Peter Navarro, who responded by asking whether Carney was threatening to “play China off the US”.
“This is offensive in the extreme,” he said, adding that Carney should be more worried that China would “eat Canada alive”.
Carney has made looking to markets beyond the US a central part of his economic strategy, as Trump’s tariffs hit Canadian industries, including auto manufacturing, as well as steel and aluminium.
Trade talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down in August , but Carney said on Saturday that he’d spoken with Trump and senior officials, and that while differences remained, there was progress towards a possible deal.
He also met with Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Tuesday, with both countries reaffirming their commitment to renew the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement , according to Carney’s office.
One year after Carney visited Mexico, during which they launched a strategic partnership, the two leaders agreed to keep expanding bilateral trade and investment. They also highlighted a 19-percent increase in merchandise trade in the first nine months of this year, compared with the same period last year.

articles.title_orig: Senate Democrats demand briefings about FAA ground stop amid $50B budget ask - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Senate Democrats demand briefings about FAA ground stop amid $50B budget ask - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
The funding would go to new air traffic control centers and other improvements.
Democrats on the Senate Commerce Committee sent a letter to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Federal Aviation Administration's Bryan Bedford on Tuesday demanding an explanation for Friday's nationwide ground stop and calling for briefings before there are additional changes to the air traffic control system.
It comes the same day the Department of Transportation has officially submitted its $50.1 billion budget funding request -- a marked increase -- to fix a system Duffy and President Donald Trump say is broken . The budget breakdown includes more than $10 billion for the completion of a reliable digital architecture, more than $10 billion to overhaul outdated airport infrastructure, $10 billion to build five new air traffic control centers and another $10 billion to build and improve up to 140 air traffic control towers.
Duffy has said the $50 billion funding ask, which is in addition to the $12.5 billion that was appropriated by Congress, is needed to fix the issues that led to the ground stop.
"This is an emergency," he told reporters Friday night. "I want Congress to give us emergency funding. This is bipartisan. This is American. I want $50 billion."
In their letter, Democrats said that Friday's ground stop "disrupted air travel across the country, eroded public trust in our aviation system, and raised serious questions" about the FAA and its ability to ensure reliable operations.
"Congress expects clear, fact-based answers about the root cause of this disruption and why existing safeguards failed to prevent it," the 13 Democrats on the committee wrote in the letter.
The senators addressed Duffy's funding request -- noting that the increase from $30 billion to $50 billion following Friday's ground stop "is notably $20 billion more than the request from DOT and the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) that was sent on Thursday, November 12."
"DOT, FAA and OMB must provide Congress with a complete account of what happened and how additional funding would address the vulnerabilities presented on November 13," the senators wrote.
Ahead of a meeting with Duffy on Tuesday, Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said the funding request needs to be detailed.
"If you want $30 billion or $50 billion, you better damn sure have a long list of initiatives and planning that went into it versus ‘give me a number and I'll figure out how to spend it.’”
GOP Sen. John Cornyn said when it comes to FAA funding, he would like to know "what they have, why they haven't spent it and why they need more."
The Democratic senators also raised questions about devices from Juniper -- the company that manufactured the routers believed to be central to the ground stop -- as well as L3 Harris, a government contractor that provides technology and IT support for the FAA and that worked with Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Juniper to install the routers.
The ground stop happened because of a telecommunications issue, both Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on Friday; FAA Administrator Bedford added that it was the result of faulty equipment.
Duffy told ABC's "This Week" Sunday that work was being done to replace outdated copper wire with fiber cables in El Dorado, Arkansas, when the router communication believed to have caused the ground stop occurred. When the router in that area was turned on, "we saw that in Amarillo, Texas, a system we had replaced about three weeks earlier, that started to flood our system as well," Duffy explained.
In the letter, the senators requested a pause on the installation of additional Juniper devices -- the devices that are replacing routers in the copper-to-fiber transition -- until further testing demonstrates that they can be deployed safely.
The lawmakers say they expect a briefing on those improvements before installation continues.
"Deployment should resume after the FAA demonstrates the devices' readiness for safe deployment through improved operational testing, independent validation, verified failover capability, and rollback procedures," they said.
The FAA announced Tuesday afternoon that it was halting the installation of Juniper routers .
The senators requested technical briefings from the FAA, L3 Harris and Juniper by Monday. Those briefings should include an initial safety assessment and explanations about how the system lacked sufficient redundancy to immediately recover during Friday's ground stop, the senators wrote in the letter.
The outage, they write, has left them "concerned" about DOT's ability to oversee the new air traffic control system.
"Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety," they wrote.
Asked for comment on the letter, a DOT spokesperson said "The Department has provided updates as we have them and will continue to do so."
Sen. Tammy Duckworth, the ranking member of the Commerce Aviation, Space and Innovation subcommittee who is among the Democrats who signed the letter, has said Duffy is "unfit to serve" in his role if he is not able to answer questions about the ground stop.
"If the Secretary cannot take responsibility and provide answers, he is unfit to serve as the Secretary of Transportation," Duckworth said in a statement to Politico.
Trump has praised Duffy amid concern over the ground stop, saying on Monday that Duffy is "doing a great job."
ABC News' Lalee Ibssa contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: A 2-month lull ends with Iran’s third strike on US targets in Bahrain
articles.title_zh: A 2-month lull ends with Iran’s third strike on US targets in Bahrain
articles.content_orig:
By Nayera Abdallah, Jana Choukeir and Phil Stewart
DUBAI, Nov 17 (Reuters) - The US and Iran exchanged fire on Tuesday, with the US striking an Iranian missile launch site after Iran said it targeted a US military radar system in Bahrain, despite talks between Iran and mediators Oman and Qatar.
The latest back-and-forth between the US and Iran ‌was a reminder of difficulties ending nearly nine months of war that have destabilised the Middle East, pushed up global energy prices and fueled US voter anger in November ‌elections that punished President Donald Trump's Republican Party.
A US military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said US fighter jets fired on a Revolutionary Guards missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz in response to Iran's "aggression targeting ​US personnel and assets." Iranian media, citing an Iranian official, said the US attack did not damage infrastructure.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said earlier on Tuesday they targeted a US military radar system at Bahrain's Sheikh Isa base, and warned Bahrain over its alliance with the US and stance towards Shi'ite clergy.
Bahrain, which is home to the headquarters of the US Fifth Fleet, said it intercepted the attack and there were no reports of casualties or damage.
Qatari and Iranian officials met on Tuesday for talks aimed at "bridging perspectives and narrowing the gap between proposals presented on the ground," Qatari spokesperson Majed Al Ansari said.
They coincide with a visit to ‌Oman by Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi. Oman's Foreign Ministry said he ⁠discussed safeguarding maritime corridors and ensuring the smooth flow of global shipping and trade, as well as preventing military escalation, with Oman's foreign minister.
Oman and Iran lie on opposite sides of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital waterway that carried about one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies before ⁠the war but is now partly blocked by Iran.
Oman has previously held talks with Tehran about controlling traffic in the strait.
Araqchi said in a post on Telegram that he also met Oman's Sultan Haitham bin Tariq and informed him about Iran's diplomatic initiative to end the war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
RISE IN ATTACKS ON TANKERS
The war has ground to a stalemate, with Trump saying he might ​hold ​off from attacking Iran if the US does not face what he described as provocations from Tehran or the ​Iran-backed Houthi group in Yemen.
Trump said on Tuesday the US was taking seriously ‌the possibility that Iran could be planning an attack involving a dirty bomb in Washington, after being asked about a CNN report citing US intelligence assessments.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson said the report was part of a US campaign "to lay the media groundwork for their sinister designs" using "baseless allegations."
Trump has also said he will maintain a US naval blockade on Iran because it has continued to disrupt shipping in the strait, which is a sticking point in negotiations.
Attacks on tankers have increased this month in the strait, and the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said the crew of a tanker passing through the waterway was unaccounted for after being attacked north of the Omani port city of Khasab.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards and navy said on Tuesday that a ship carrying LNG and two oil tankers ‌had caught fire in the strait. Reuters could not independently verify the reports.
Benchmark Brent crude futures were up 0.4% ​at $92.76 a barrel, much higher than before the war but well below April's wartime peak of $126.41.
The war continues to spill ​over into other parts of the Middle East as Iran puts pressure on Washington ​through its Houthi allies, who have carried out attacks on Saudi Arabia and seized areas along the Yemeni coast on the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, hoping to squeeze Gulf ‌oil producers.
Tuesday's attack on Bahrain, a Shi'ite-majority country ruled by a Sunni ​Muslim family, followed the sentencing there of 64 people, ​mostly Shi'ite clerics, to life in prison on charges of colluding with Iran to undermine the state.
Iran's Foreign Ministry condemned the court's ruling on Tuesday and said the accusations were baseless. Tehran has long denied interference in Bahrain's internal affairs.
Iran also fired on Bahrain on Sunday, saying it had targeted a US radar system at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base following what ​it said were hostile US actions.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi ‌said Bahrain had made "three key mistakes," which he listed as "cooperating in the invasion of the Islamic Republic of Iran, remaining within the US security bubble, and encroaching on the ​sanctity of Shi'ite religious authority."
These, "if continued, will jeopardize its survival in the region's new security order," Mohebbi said.
(Additional reporting by Yomna Ehab and Elwely Elwelly, Writing by ​Nayera Abdallah, Aidan Lewis and Phil Stewart; Editing by Ros Russell, Peter Graff, Don Durfee and Rod Nickel)

articles.title_zh: Latin American leaders get face time with China at APEC Summit 2026
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.
Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.
Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms.
“For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University.
US-Taiwan ties remain strong behind the scenes
Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan.
One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity.
“This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.
The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion.
The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t.
“I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.”
Stalled arms sales for now
Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.
Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.
Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.
But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.
Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low.
“I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said.
China expands coast guard role in pressure on Taiwan
Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.
Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan’s National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.
The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025.
“I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off” Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.
These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China’s claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan’s east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan’s outlying islands closer to China.
Wang compared the approach to Beijing’s tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection.
“It’s telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.”

articles.title_orig: Memo to Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress: Remind the world why you've been Jensen Huang's CFO for 13-plus years
articles.title_zh: Memo to Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress: Remind the world why you've been Jensen Huang's CFO for 13-plus years
articles.content_orig:
Nobody—not even Nvidia’s board—knows who will lead the new regime at Nvidia now that Jensen Huang is gone . For now, longtime CFO Colette Kress is in the driver’s seat as interim chief, and she’s been handed Atlas’s job of holding up the sky during Nvidia’s fiscal 2027 third quarter results after the bell on Tuesday.
Kress has to be the “voice of stability” while she also attempts to get the investment community reoriented to the fundamental issues at Nvidia that impact the business and valuation of the stock, said Melissa Otto, global head of Visible Alpha Research at S&P Global.
First and foremost, analysts are still expecting a typically gargantuan quarter, with $109.3 billion in revenue, according to S&P’s Visible Alpha consensus—which is routine for Nvidia and will be mission critical for Kress. The quarterly figure is up about 92% from $57 billion last year, but the number has to be delivered in the right way. Nvidia’s gotten the world used to over performance and now the company needs to sizzle with confidence at one of the most vulnerable moments in its history.
“There’s a complete evaporation of confidence at the moment, and there’s so much uncertainty around a lot of qualitative issues,” said Otto. “The narrative needs to come back to fundamentals. How is the business doing? Is it achieving what it said it’s going to achieve?”
Nvidia’s stock is down 20% since the company’s last quarterly earnings on August 26, losing roughly half a trillion dollars in market cap, amid a broader selloff in AI and related tech stocks that have since rallied. Tuesday could be a moment for Nvidia to make its case (or at least, its first impression) as a post-Jensen business. Or it could be a bloodbath.
Here are six key things to pay attention on Nvidia’s earnings conference call.
Nvidia told investors in August to expect third-quarter revenue of $108 billion, plus or minus 2%, which puts us in the range of about $105.8 billion to $110.2 billion. That outlook assumed no data center compute revenue from China.
Visible Alpha consensus sits at $109.3 billion with earnings of $2.47 per share. The data center segment—Nvidia’s crown jewel—is expected to deliver $101.8 billion of the topline total, with estimates ranging from $99.7 billion to $110.8 billion. Nvidia’s third quarter ended in late October, which means the results were not affected by Huang’s ouster. Still, any signs of weakness in the business during Huang’s final days at the helm would likely add even more uncertainty to the company’s prospects.
Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets, wrote in commentary that the earnings report “will be a major referendum on the AI trade following its leadership shake-up, particularly its outlook for demand, margins and financial commitments.” Colossal results “won’t resolve the questions surrounding Jensen’s departure,” he wrote.
This is Otto’s top issue. “Do they maintain their guidance for next year?” she said. “If that’s not the case, then there’s going to be some volatility.” That’s putting it lightly.
In August, Kress said Nvidia’s preliminary expectation was for revenue to grow about 70% in fiscal 2028 (roughly equivalent to calendar 2027), with supply remaining a bottleneck at least through the end of next year.
At the time, Huang said Nvidia had never guided financial figures a year in advance, but with demand running well above 70%, he felt confident about it. The true test will be whether that confidence outlives his ouster.
“It is the case that we’ve never forecasted or never guided to a year in advance,” said Huang at the time. “And even though our demand is much greater than 70%, our supply allows us to confidently deliver 70%.”
That means $699.2 billion in fiscal 2028 revenue, if Huang’s confidence holds up, according to Visible Alpha’s revenue consensus. In the official announcement of Huang’s resignation last week, Nvidia’s newly installed board chair, Harvey Jones, said the company expects “operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption.” We’ll see.
For now, it’s Kress and the board has said it will consider internal and external candidates to replace Huang , whether that’s one person, or a sharing of power in multiple new roles. Otto called the leadership transition “essentially a regime change” and said investors want to hear what comes next.
“What changes might be made and how might this affect their existing strategy?” she said.
There are also constituencies, mainly other tech founders, who want to see Huang return to his CEO role . Portfolio managers don’t love holding stock that tanks, especially a stock that has been such a rocket ship: Nvidia shares have surged more than 1,300% since ChatGPT’s late 2022 launch.
“For a company that spent 33 years under one CEO, this is about more than beating expectations,” Woods wrote. “Nvidia now needs to show that the business can continue delivering without the man who built it.”
Giuseppe Sette, cofounder and president of Reflexivity, wrote in commentary that a reinstatement “would most likely trigger a sharp, immediate relief rally,” but on a “less durable and more volatile path than the classic founder-return analogues, since this is a scandal-driven exit rather than a strategy-driven one.”
Nvidia has become an important financial backer of its customers , through direct investments and guarantees to backstop debt, with neocloud companies ranking among the biggest beneficiaries.
Total future commitments, spread over the next five fiscal years and thereafter, amount to $366 billion, with $120 billion falling in the remainder of fiscal 2027, which ends in late January. Supply and capacity makes up $279 billion of that total, up from $119 billion the quarter before.
John Belton of Gabelli Funds wrote that the initiatives are “polarizing for the stock giving ongoing concerns about ‘circular financing.’”
Recent media reports have suggested that Kress, and Huang himself prior to his exit, were rethinking Nvidia’s role as the AI industry’s “central bank” and were planning to tighten the purse strings.
Mark Malek, chief investment officer at Siebert Financial, said the AI trade splits two ways. “Those collecting checks for building the future and those writing the checks hoping the future eventually pays them back—investors had better know which ones they own.”
Nvidia’s market success rests on the strength of its technology, so it’s crucial that it flawlessly execute the baton pass from its current Blackwell product line up to Vera Rubin, Nvidia’s newer, next generation platform.
“This is the year,” said S&P’s Otto. “We’ve seen Blackwell doing quite well, and what we would want to understand is how should we be thinking about Rubin for the rest of this year and next year.”
In August, Nvidia said Rubin was ramping into full production, with server racks running at partners including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle , and Nebius. In August, Kress said Rubin would account for about 20% of data center revenue in the third quarter, and that hyperscale growth would reaccelerate in the fourth quarter and into fiscal 2028 as Rubin supply spreads.
Otto said she’s got her ears pricked for “any kind of color” that shows whether expectations “are aligned correctly to the way that they’re describing the market.”
In August, Nvidia lowered the bar for gross profit margin expectations, blaming the industry-wide rise in memory prices. It guided to a third-quarter gross margin of 74%, plus or minus 50 basis points, down from 75% in the second quarter.
Kress told investors  at the time that margins would “bottom” in the fourth quarter at 71% to 72%, then settle at 72% to 73% as Nvidia’s own product price increases take effect. “We want to be direct about this rather than let it linger as an open question,” said Kress.

articles.title_orig: Civilization studio Firaxis Games lays off a third of staff
articles.title_zh: Civilization studio Firaxis Games lays off a third of staff
articles.content_orig:
Firaxis Games, the studio behind the Civilization and XCOM franchises of computer strategy games, last week laid off about a third of its staff, totaling around 60 people. That’s according to a recent report in Bloomberg.
The report cites people “familiar with the cuts,” saying that the flagship game the studio is currently working on, a new entry in the XCOM series, “has faced development struggles and missed a significant milestone.” The departures also include the studio head, Heather Hazen.
A Firaxis spokesperson released the following statement:
Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength—designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years. As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis.
The storied studio has had a rough run of things of late. Its most recent game, Civilization VII , launched to solid enough sales but divided players in terms of reception. Players have long criticized new Civilization titles for being barebones compared to immediate predecessors that have seen multiple post-launch updates and expansions, but the response was sharper this time.
The game has found more fans in recent months , but a portion of the Civilization audience will likely never fully warm to it due to its ages system—a design choice that partially solved many long-standing pacing problems, but at the cost of altering the core experience.
Before that, Firaxis worked on Marvel’s Midnight Suns , which had a more positive reception in terms of sentiment but does not seem to have sold as many units as the company had hoped. Now, with the new XCOM title facing challenges, that’s three troubled games in a row.
To top it off, most of Firaxis’ direct competitors in the strategy game market are much leaner and not beholden to a major publisher. (The publisher for the Civilization franchise is 2K Games, which lives under the same company that publishes the soon-to-launch Grand Theft Auto VI .)
The industry at large has seen widespread layoffs and studio closures over the past few years. There’s no single reason for that; rather, there are numerous factors, including contraction after COVID-era over-investment, increased competition, changes in leadership culture at major publishers, and larger economic factors beyond the scope of just the games industry.

articles.title_orig: Ukraine Attacks Kerch Bridge Linking Russia to Occupied Crimea
articles.title_zh: Ukraine Attacks Kerch Bridge Linking Russia to Occupied Crimea
articles.content_orig:
With the SpaceX satellite system faltering, Ukraine’s military launched a surprise, multi-pronged attack to take down vital bridge to Crimea
A t 10pm on Monday evening a Ukrainian soldier scrawled a message on a kamikaze drone. It said simply: “The bridge is fucked.” He then added: “We will stand and Moscow will fall.” It was a freezing night, with a bright starry sky and no clouds. Lines of ice had formed on the drone’s bulky wings. Soon, it would be hurtling towards its target – about 500km to the south.
Typically the soldiers who gathered in this muddy field in central Ukraine were attacking oil refineries deep inside Russia. In recent months the work had become almost mundane: they had hit so many of them. The objective that evening, however, was unique. It was a structure personally associated with Vladimir Putin and his grandiose imperial ambitions.
“We knew what the target was. Everyone was enthusiastic and excited,” one person who took part in the special operation, using the pseudonym “Leon”, told the Guardian. His 7th Deep Strike Centre is part of “Magyar’s Birds”, a brigade named after the call sign of its founder, Robert Brovdi, the head of Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces . Leon said: “Nobody gets excited any more about oil refineries. This was different.”
The soldiers got ready to launch, then watched the biplane-like drone, laden with explosives, disappear across the southern Ukrainian steppe.
Over the next four hours, hundreds of attack drones followed the same linear path, flying first over land and then over the Black Sea. In the early hours of the morning they arrived at their destination: the Kerch bridge connecting occupied Crimea with Russia. Putin opened the monumental road and rail crossing in 2018 , driving across it in a Kamaz truck. This was four years after his undercover troops – known as little green men – seized the peninsula.
Russian propagandists had described the bridge as impregnable. It was, they said, an edifice as strong and unyielding as their country’s iron leader. For Ukraine , by contrast, it was a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Also, officials pointed out, it was illegal. Twice Kyiv had tried to blow it up – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.
On this occasion, the Ukrainian military’s careful, multi-stage plan worked perfectly. “It was a well-coordinated operation. Waves of drones started from different locations. The goal was to overwhelm Russia’s well-organised air defence system, rather than the bridge itself,” Leon explained.
As expected, the initial salvo tied up Russia’s local defences. According to insiders, Ukraine then launched a second drone wave. Its function was crucial and different: to act as a relay system for radio signals. Previously, Ukrainian units had used Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, for mid-range strikes on occupied territory. Elon Musk’s SpaceX owns the satellite internet network, which is overseen by the Pentagon and the Trump administration.
Ten days ago, however, limits were mysteriously imposed on Ukrainian drones, so they could no longer fly at above 161 km/h (100 mph) . SpaceX insists there is no slowdown – a statement Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, says is untrue . On Monday night, it appears Kyiv bypassed US restrictions by setting up its own extraordinary and innovative real-time video and radio connection.
Once the relay was in place, a third wave of attacks could begin. This time they featured Flamingos, a potent Ukrainian-made cruise missile capable of carrying 1,000kg of explosives – enough to seriously damage the bridge. An unknown number of missiles – some reports say at least four – were launched from southern Ukraine and sent towards Crimea.
A video from one of the Flamingos shows it drawing inexorably towards the target. The onboard camera captures a ghostly night-time scene. The crossing looms into view against a grisaille background. Suddenly a gigantic steel arch appears. The feed cuts out. Other footage shows the moment of impact: an orange fireball, pricking the surrounding blackness.
Photos taken on Tuesday morning in the aftermath of the attack show a scene of watery devastation. A massive arch had tumbled overnight into the Kerch straight , with a large concrete chunk of the road crossing. Nobody will be driving across the bridge anytime soon. The adjacent railway arch span was also damaged. “We were very happy, swapping messages all night,” Leon said.
One source in Ukraine’s armed forces said the timing of the operation – hailed by Zelenskyy as “unprecedented” – was deliberate. It was conducted ahead of a meeting on Thursday between Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Putin in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, on the sidelines of an Apec summit. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” the person said.
They added: “We understand that what we did shows the world that the king is nude. Putin is weak and vulnerable and we just proved it. The operation was purposefully designed for this specific historic moment. Putin’s plan was to bluff at the summit about how powerful he is. In reality, he can’t even protect the most important and symbolic pillars of his regime.”
In addition to Putin’s political embarrassment before his peers, the disabling of the Kerch bridge has practical consequences. Since annexing Crimea, Russia has militarised the peninsula, effectively turning it into a giant and fortified army base. Since 2022 it has been used as a launch platform for drone and missile attacks on the port of Odesa, and other Ukrainian cities in the region.
Russia’s occupying southern army has relied on the bridge for regular deliveries of ammunition, equipment and fuel. With the crossing partially closed – rail travel reportedly reopened on Tuesday – Russia will have to use an under fire land corridor instead, connecting its Rostov oblast with the Moscow-controlled parts of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces.
“We have disrupted their logistics to Crimea. There will be a lot of problems for Russia’s army in the south,” Leon predicted. Debris from the bridge strike is obstructing the narrow shipping corridor through the Kerch strait, linking the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea. The Azov sea now resembles a lake. Passenger ferries are unable to move, with the occupied ports of Mariupol and Berdyansk cut off.
The soldiers returned from their mission jubilant and elated. Back at their headquarters, they gathered as usual for a minute’s silence, in memory of those killed in Russia’s bloody war. “We had our daily ritual as usual. Then there were congratulations on a very successful and important operation,” Leon said. Then he added: “We are paying them back.”

articles.title_orig: How to Tell If It’s a Cyberattack or Just an Outage
articles.title_zh: How to Tell If It’s a Cyberattack or Just an Outage
articles.content_orig:
Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.
Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies , a Federal Aviation Administration tech screwup grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking , this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.
Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.
The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.
“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”
So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.
The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.
As the head of internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One's default position should be that it isn't a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”
Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”
In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services , for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.
In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.
On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.
It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech company may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.
Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with issues. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS , Google Cloud Platform , and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products , Google Workspace , telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.
When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon —but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net . Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his social media accounts .
When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.
Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what's actually going on,” she says.
Most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.
Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. articles.title_orig: Framework’s better couch keyboard is now available for preorder
articles.title_zh: Framework’s better couch keyboard is now available for preorder
articles.content_orig:
Logitech’s K400 may have met its match.﻿
Logitech’s K400 may have met its match.﻿
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
Framework announced its Wireless Touchpad Keyboard earlier this year with the goal of delivering a better couch keyboarding experience than the Logitech K400 . According to The Verge ’s Sean Hollister who went hands-on with Framework’s new all-in-one keyboard and touchpad last April, the company has succeeded in that goal, but it turns out you’ll be paying a bit more for Framework’s than Logitech’s.
While the K400 couch keyboard is $35, the Framework Wireless Touchpad Keyboard is $99 with a $50 fully refundable deposit required to preorder one starting today . That makes it nearly three times more expensive than Logitech’s, but Framework’s upgrades and improvements could make it worth the premium.
Instead of starting from scratch, Framework uses the same keyboard module found in its Laptop 12 paired with a precision 120Hz touchpad and controller that’s also used in all of the company’s computers. A Bluetooth connection is the easiest way to pair the keyboard to PCs running Windows, Linux, or macOS, or mobile devices, game consoles, and streaming boxes. You can quickly switch between four wirelessly connected devices with a button press including one that uses an included USB receiver. If you want more responsiveness, you can also tether it to a device with a USB-C cable.
On a full charge of its replaceable 1,200mAh battery the keyboard will run for well over a year with sporadic use. If you’re instead using it for hours every day on a desk, Framework estimates the battery life will be closer to over a month. For customizability and remapping the keyboard’s open source firmware is based on a fork of ZMK .

articles.title_orig: Nasdaq 100 Futures Rise as Investors Prepare for Nvidia Results
articles.title_zh: Nasdaq 100 Futures Rise as Investors Prepare for Nvidia Results
articles.content_orig:
A major week for Wall Street started on a down note. US markets closed lower Monday, led by declines in technology stocks associated with the artificial intelligence boom.
The S&P 500 fell 1.9%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 2.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 739 points, or 1.4%. Wall Street’s fear gauge, the VIX, surged 19%.
Shares of Nvidia ( NVDA ) dropped 4.1%, falling for the third consecutive day since Jensen Huang resigned. Nvidia shares are coming off their worst week in 19 months. Investors are gearing up for Nvidia’s quarterly earnings report, expected Tuesday after the market close.
Shares of the semiconductor chip designer have had a rocky few weeks, with the Huang scandal accelerating declines. Nvidia shares are down roughly 35% since a record high on October 6, erasing about $2 trillion in market value.
On Monday, shares of Nvidia closed at $156.14, their lowest level since July 1, 2025. Nvidia shares have erased all of their gains over the past 16 months. Nvidia stock was hit by a raft of Wall Street analysts slashing their price targets last week. At Evercore ISI, analysts cut their price target to $186, down from a prior target of $465. At HSBC, analysts cut their target to $170, down from $365.
Shares of semiconductor chipmakers, Big Tech and other companies involved in the data center buildout fell Monday. Intel shares ( INTC ) fell 7.1%, while Alphabet shares ( GOOG ) fell 3.85%. CoreWeave shares ( CRWV ) sank 6.1%.
The Commerce Department on Monday also tightened export controls designed to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips. The much-anticipated Commerce rule puts new curbs on US exports to data centers that provide “significant volumes” of computing to companies based in countries subject to US arms embargoes, such as China, Iran and Russia.
The Dow, S&P 500 and Nasdaq each gained more than 2% last week. The declines on Monday ate away at those gains. Overall, the S&P and Nasdaq are down roughly 5% and 11%, respectively, since record highs on October 6. The Dow is down 5% since its peak on August 5.
Investors are also gearing up for Anthropic’s expected initial public offering later this week. The AI frontier lab is targeting a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion , and its IPO is a pivotal moment for the tech boom that has become a driving force for the US stock market.
“How investors view Nvidia’s updates against the recent turmoil left in the wake of Jensen Huang’s departure and the market reaction to Anthropic becoming a public company may determine whether the AI trade can gain its footing or whether hiccups here cause further damage across the ecosystem,” Anthony Saglimbene, chief market strategist at Ameriprise Financial, wrote in a Monday note.

articles.title_orig: Russian military plane crashes in Siberia killing all 19 on board
articles.title_zh: Russian military plane crashes in Siberia killing all 19 on board
articles.content_orig:
A Russian military transport plane has crashed in Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, the country's defence ministry said, according to state-run media.
The An-12 aircraft went down during a "scheduled flight" in an "uninhabited area" in the Kemerovo region, the ministry said in a statement.
The ministry added that it preliminarily believed a technical malfunction was the cause of Tuesday's crash. An investigation by Russia's aviation authorities is now under way.
Local Governor Ilya Seredyuk said an emergency response team "quickly extinguished a blaze" after the crash near the village of Yagunovo, and the area was sealed off by police.
Seredyuk, who visited the crash site, said "a helicopter and medical facilities have been put on standby".
The governor added that the "main task" now was to help investigators carry out their work.
He also posted a video showing firefighters combing through what looked like the crash debris, with a number of ambulances also seen standing nearby.
CCTV footage posted on social media appeared to show the moment the plane crashed, with a lighted object falling through the sky in the distance. An explosion then lit up the sky, but the crash was too far away to be seen.
The BBC and Reuters news agency verified the time and date of the footage, while Reuters also verified the location based on features of the scenery that matched satellite imagery of the area.
It was not immediately known whether the crashed aircraft had any cargo on board.
An-12 planes are widely used by the Russian military to transport weaponry and personnel, and also for search and rescue operations.

articles.title_orig: Apple reports outages after an internal update, says it is working to get systems back online
articles.title_zh: Apple reports outages after an internal update, says it is working to get systems back online
articles.content_orig:
Apple said it was experiencing tech issues Tuesday that were affecting several of its popular consumer-facing services.
As of 2 p.m. ET, Apple’s own system status page showed that Apple Business, Apple School Manager, AppleCare, iCloud Mail and Web Apps, and SchoolWork were each experiencing outages.
Earlier, the page showed the App Store and Apple Music  experiencied outages.
“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” an Apple spokesperson told NBC News. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”
At Apple stores in New York and Chicago, employees told NBC News earlier in the day that their internal software had stopped working and they had been unable to complete purchases or make appointments.
Over the past week, U.S. residents have experienced a cascade of technical issues that have led to nationwide outages of key consumer services, including email, air travel and online banking.
While none of the issues appear to be related, they’ve exposed America’s reliance on older infrastructure and revealed the extent to which companies and governments are being forced to upgrade systems in the AI age. The incidents have also stoked unfounded paranoia that something larger may be afoot.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI’s New Hacking Model Found Dozens Of Holes In Apple Tech
articles.title_zh: OpenAI’s New Hacking Model Found Dozens Of Holes In Apple Tech
articles.content_orig:
A viral post credits OpenAI with 35 Apple bugs, but Apple's own patch notes tie the company's Codex Security tool to three WebKit fixes
Tue 17 Nov 2026 · 14:29 EST · 3 min read
A post circulating on X claims a new OpenAI model found 35 vulnerabilities in Apple devices. The post says some of those flaws could let hackers take control of iPhones and Macs.
The post on X does not name the model or break down the 35 bugs. It describes the haul as covering iPhones and Macs, and it frames some of the flaws as serious enough to allow remote control of those devices.
Research into the claim found no confirmed reports of an OpenAI model identifying exactly 35 vulnerabilities across Apple hardware. The figure does not appear in Apple’s published security credits.
What does appear is this. In June 2026, Apple shipped security updates for iOS, iPadOS, macOS and Safari. Those updates addressed over 30 flaws, and AI tools assisted in the process.
Three of those fixes stand out. Apple credited OpenAI Codex Security with three vulnerabilities in WebKit, the engine underneath Safari.
So the confirmed tally attributed directly to OpenAI is three, not 35. The “over 30” figure belongs to the full June patch batch, which drew on AI assistance more broadly.
The June updates were not routine housekeeping. The urgency behind them was driven by concern that AI is speeding up the pace at which attackers develop hacking techniques.
Apple accelerated its patch release timelines after recognizing that increased risk.

We respect your privacy. Unsubscribe anytime.
The Apple credits are a small piece of a larger effort. In November 2026, OpenAI announced that an autonomous cybersecurity pipeline had identified 948 distinct Linux kernel local privilege-escalation vulnerabilities.
A privilege-escalation bug is the digital equivalent of a visitor’s badge that somehow opens the server room. An attacker who already has limited access to a system uses the flaw to grab much deeper control.
The pipeline did not stop at finding those bugs. According to OpenAI’s announcement, it also generated exploits and patches for them.
The run happened in October and reportedly cost approximately $1.2 million in API credits. For a sweep that produced 948 distinct kernel flaws along with fixes, that is a notable demonstration of how much ground automated tooling can now cover.
For all the alarming numbers, there is a reassuring detail. To date, no major security breaches have been tied back to these findings.
For Apple users, the practical lesson is simple. The June 2026 updates covered iOS, iPadOS, macOS and Safari, and the window between a bug being found and being weaponized appears to be shrinking.
For Apple, the episode shows a company adjusting its release rhythm to match a faster threat cycle. Crediting an AI tool in official security notes also signals that machine-found bugs are now a normal part of the pipeline, not a novelty.
For OpenAI, the security work doubles as a capability showcase. The Linux kernel results and the WebKit credits give the company concrete evidence that its models can do useful defensive work.
The viral 35 figure may not hold up against the record. The trend it gestures at, AI tools finding real flaws in widely used software and vendors racing to keep up, very much does.

articles.title_orig: Kalshi halts trading on Trump's speeches
articles.title_zh: Kalshi halts trading on Trump's speeches
articles.content_orig:
Prediction market platform Kalshi quietly paused trading in a handful of "mention" contracts tied to President Donald Trump at the end of last week at the request of the CFTC, the company confirmed on Tuesday.
Mention markets are made up of contracts that ask traders what specific words will be used in a speech, a corporate earnings call or during a television broadcast.  Earlier this year, a White House teleprompter operator used inside information to place trades in mention markets related to the president's comments.
Markets paused include those asking traders what nicknames Trump will say before 2027, what the president will say in November and what countries and companies Trump will say before the end of the month.
The move comes after the Commodity Futures Trading Commission , the federal agency overseeing prediction markets, said in a letter to exchanges in September that mentions contracts have a greater manipulation risk.
A spokesperson for the agency told CNBC that the commission has placed holds on the certification of some of Kalshi's proposed mention markets. The spokesperson cited a Kalshi contract on hold that asked what key words would Trump say before a certain date. The contract was originally self-certified by Kalshi in February 2025.
"The CFTC stayed the certification of these contracts because they may be susceptible to manipulation, which is consistent with the staff advisory the CFTC put out two months ago," said Brooke Nethercott, the agency's spokesperson.
In a statement, Kalshi spokesperson Dani Lever said Kalshi is complying with the order.
In August, reports emerged that the CFTC was conducting an internal review into mention markets. The agency also requested that Kalshi, which is the only U.S.-regulated exchange that features the contract type, take down its sports-related mention markets in response to the inquiry. Kalshi complied.
A Trump-related mention market drew scrutiny in July after it was revealed a White House teleprompter operator placed trades on markets related to the president's comments. In a settlement with the operator, the CFTC ordered a three-year trading ban on the individual and a penalty amounting to over $172,000 .
Kalshi has defended mentions markets even as the CFTC has become increasingly skeptical of them, saying that the individual words of prominent people often cause billions of dollars of movement across financial markets.
In addition to scrutiny regarding mention markets, the company is also facing a probe from the CFTC about its communications about new products with the agency, though a spokesperson for the company told CNBC that it was working to resolve the issues.
As of Tuesday morning, a mention market asking what Vice President JD Vance would say during the New York Times DealBook Summit event on Wednesday is still active.

articles.title_orig: Pentagon detains US soldier accused of spying at British base
articles.title_zh: Pentagon detains US soldier accused of spying at British base
articles.content_orig:
The US military has detained an American soldier accused of spying for Russia at a UK military base.
The senior officer, identified by The Telegraph as Lt Col Brandon Tyner, was first detained by UK counter-terrorism police in Gloucestershire on Nov 10.
On Tuesday, the 41-year-old was taken into custody by the US military over suspected national security and espionage allegations , according to the Metropolitan Police.
Asst Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of counter terrorism policing (CTP) in the UK, said: “Following an extensive investigation, CTP presented our case to the CPS, who in turn engaged with the Attorney General’s Office and American partners. Subsequently, a decision was made to pass the investigation to them to progress.”
He added: “These are extremely serious allegations, and our collective response should send a strong message that we will act swiftly and robustly where we suspect this kind of espionage activity taking place.”
He said UK police would “continue to support our US colleagues as they take the matter forwards”.
Kash Patel, the director of the FBI, said: “This FBI has zero tolerance for anyone who betrays their oath to the United States or puts our national security at risk.”
Lt Col Tyner’s arrest followed a long-running investigation by British and American authorities, including MI5 and the FBI.
It is believed to be the first time a US soldier has been arrested on suspicion of spying offences on British soil.
Lt Col Tyner was assigned to Nato’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps. He joined the US army in 2008 and served in Iraq, Afghanistan and Qatar, according to a US army official.
The Telegraph understands that he is suspected of sharing intelligence that would be highly damaging in the hands of a foreign power. However, officials are confident that no intelligence left the base.
It is believed that the soldier volunteered his services to Moscow, but was allegedly ensnared by undercover officers posing as Russian operatives.
Officials said his alleged motive was not clear.
He was based at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth, the headquarters of the Nato Allied Rapid Reaction Corps and the UK’s largest Nato base.
Commanded by the British Army, the site hosts service members from more than 20 alliance nations. It holds a readiness force capable of deploying tens of thousands of troops on short notice and recently participated in an exercise modelling the defence of Europe.
An army official said Lt Col Tyner was expected to be prosecuted under the US Uniform Code of Military Justice.
Brig Gen Sean Stinchon, the commander general of the US military’s counter-intelligence command, said: “This case should serve as a stark warning to any service member suspected of violating the oath we all take to protect and defend the Constitution.”
Lt Col Tyner enlisted as a senior human resources officer in January 2008, a military official told The Telegraph.
He earned a bronze star for overseas deployment, having served in Iraq from December 2019 to July 2020, Qatar from July 2016 to July 2017 and Afghanistan from December 2013 to December 2014.
He was promoted to the rank of major in 2018 and lieutenant colonel in 2024.
The serviceman has regularly posted about cryptocurrency online. He also states on his social media that he volunteered at Burning Man festival, and describes himself as a “change agent”.
In his LinkedIn profile, Lt Col Tyner describes himself as a “disruptor” who “thrive[s] in high energy, ever evolving organisations with passions for diversity, growth, and cultural fitness”.

articles.title_orig: Why 'Shark Tank' star Kevin O'Leary wouldn't bring Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO
articles.title_zh: Why 'Shark Tank' star Kevin O'Leary wouldn't bring Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
'Shark Tank' star and veteran investor Kevin O'Leary isn't aligning himself with the prominent voices calling for Nvidia ( NVDA ) to bring back Jensen Huang as CEO — a growing crowd in the billionaire land that is Silicon Valley.
"No, no, no, that's not going to happen. That will not happen," O'Leary said on Sozzi Unleashed . "It probably will never happen, because over the next two years, the amount of scrutiny this company is going to go through during this administration's microscope on it for the whole Chinese issue, you have so many agencies launching investigations domestically and internationally. I mean, you've got Treasury and Commerce at loggerheads right now. There's just too much noise to make that move."
The man who founded Nvidia ( NVDA ) in 1993 and turned it into the most important company in the AI revolution was ousted as CEO a week ago, following a period of explosive revelations and mounting controversy.
According to the New York Times, Huang's reported relationship with a woman suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence has put Nvidia under incredible scrutiny.
The Times also reported that Huang had a relationship with Nvidia executive Kimberly Powell, one of roughly 60 people reporting directly to him. Reuters reported last Thursday that Huang had another relationship with an Nvidia employee whose identity has not been disclosed.
Huang, who has been married to his wife Lori for more than 40 years, now faces a stunning reversal for a leader whose reputation has been built on relentless execution and near-legendary control of Nvidia.
Nvidia's board reportedly has no plans to bring Huang back as CEO.
Huang broke his silence on Tuesday ahead of Nvidia's earnings release later in the afternoon.
"Since my departure, I've seen an outpouring of calls from Nvidia's employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO. If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO," Huang said in a statement .

articles.title_orig: There's 'no difference' between buying Anthropic's IPO and Amazon's IPO: Kevin O'Leary
articles.title_zh: There's 'no difference' between buying Anthropic's IPO and Amazon's IPO: Kevin O'Leary
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
As Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) prepares to begin trading under the ticker ANT on Thursday, Nov. 19, business leaders are weighing in on the historically large initial public offering (IPO).
"There's no difference in investing in Anthropic on the IPO than Amazon on its IPO," "Shark Tank" host and O'Leary Ventures chair Kevin O'Leary said on Sozzi Unleashed . "There was tremendous volatility. It made zero money. But look at the platform it ultimately built. That's what you're betting on in the Anthropic deal."
Sitting down with Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi, O'Leary said the past few years haven't been great for buying IPOs, but he believes Anthropic may be a unique way to bet on artificial intelligence.
Anthropic said it expects to sell 825 million shares priced between $70 and $78 each. That would give the company a market valuation of between $1.3 trillion and $1.45 trillion — putting it near SpaceX's ( SPCX ) IPO valuation of $1.77 trillion, which was the largest ever.
Read more: Everything you need to know ahead of Anthropic's IPO
"It may be the most hyped IPO ever," O'Leary said. "This IPO is the anchor to the entire AI or SI trade, whatever you want to call it."
What about the fact that Anthropic may not turn a profit until 2030? Though Anthropic's operating losses have improved, they still total $1.3 billion for the first nine months of the year. The company also noted in its amended IPO filing that it plans to spend nearly $900 billion on computing and data centers, with $70 billion of that total coming due within a year.
O'Leary said Anthropic's profitability is the wrong lens right now. Buying in is a bet on AI's role across all 11 sectors of the economy, and he sees evidence of productivity and margin gains so far. That has helped markets remain near all-time highs despite tariffs, wars, and high energy prices.
These remarks follow O'Leary's comments last month, when the businessman called Anthropic "a hot trade."
"I expect it to be liquid from day one, and that changes the opportunity," he wrote in October.

articles.title_orig: Sean Duffy’s attacks on past FAA ground stop resurface
articles.title_zh: Sean Duffy’s attacks on past FAA ground stop resurface
articles.content_orig:
Nearly four years before facing a nationwide FAA ground stop as transportation secretary himself, Sean Duffy criticized his predecessor in the job, then-Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, over a similar disruption in 2023, blaming incompetent leadership and misplaced “woke” priorities.
Duffy also questioned whether additional funding was needed to fix the problems, something he now says his department desperately needs.
A former Republican congressman and Fox News contributor at the time, Duffy made the comments during two Fox News appearances where he attacked the Biden administration for saying it potentially needed more money to update FAA infrastructure. Duffy also repeatedly mocked Buttigieg for taking paternity leave after adopting twins in 2021 - more than a year before the outage – and compared it with his own experience raising nine children where he boasted that he only took just “two days” off after each birth.
“They got billions of dollars, the FAA did, over COVID,” Duffy said on Fox News i n January 2023. “And now they’re gonna come back and say, ‘We want even more money to fix this crisis that we weren’t able to handle when, you know, for what, three hours in the morning aircraft couldn’t, couldn’t fly.’”
“I don’t know that it’s more money,” he added. “I think it’s just having competent people in leadership and throughout the building that can make the organization function.”
The comments stand in sharp contrast to how Duffy has talked about last week’s ground stop, which he has blamed entirely on failed, aging equipment he says won’t be fully fixed without an additional $50 billion. Whereas in 2023, Duffy repeatedly blamed the political leadership of the Biden administration, specifically Buttigieg, for that ground stop.
Asked on CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday whether he accepted responsibility for the latest outage, Duffy acknowledged his role overseeing the FAA but pointed to the aging infrastructure he inherited.
“Of course, I’m the secretary,” Duffy said. “But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me…I take responsibility for what was given to me by prior administrations.”
Duffy said the FAA was still operating with systems dating back decades and argued that the billions already approved by Congress was insufficient to complete the necessary upgrades.
Friday’s ground stop occurred after a telecommunications outage caused instability in radar data and communications with aircraft, prompting the FAA to halt departures nationwide for more than four hours. Duffy told CNN the problem appeared to emerge during routine work by contractor L3Harris to replace aging copper wire telecommunications infrastructure with fiber-optic technology.
Officials are investigating whether mistakes during that work or faulty equipment caused the failure.
The January 2023 ground stop occurred after an outage of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system, which provides pilots with critical safety information before flights. The outage prompted the agency to temporarily halt domestic departures nationwide for several hours. Investigators later determined that contractors had accidentally deleted files while working on the system’s databases.
In the hours following the January 2023 ground stop, Duffy took aim at Buttigieg during an appearance on Fox News’ America Reports , mocking his paternity leave and questioning his ability to lead the department through a crisis.
Buttigieg took approximately eight weeks of paternity leave, from mid-August to mid-October 2021, after he and his husband welcomed premature newborn twins, but the department said he was mostly offline for just the first four weeks.
“I think if Pete would stay home, go back on paternity vacation, maybe this could all just run itself,” Duffy said. “It seems when Pete shows up, things go wrong.”
“He can’t lead us through anything and doesn’t know what the problem was,” Duffy added, repeatedly and incorrectly saying Buttigieg took a “four month” leave.
During the segment, Fox News aired a live press conference where Buttigieg pledged to investigate the root cause of the outage, examine why backup systems had failed and identify what upgrades were needed to prevent another disruption.
Two days later, during a January 13 appearance on Fox News’ The Faulkner Focus , Duffy again criticized Buttigieg, accusing him of failing to identify and address weaknesses in the FAA’s aging infrastructure.
“Leadership means you look at the systems and agency in which you run, where do we have some shortcomings and where do we have to do upgrades? Pete Buttigieg hasn’t done that,” Duffy said. “Why wasn’t the money put into upgrading the FAA systems?”
In a statement to CNN, a Transportation Department spokesperson defended Duffy’s record and attacked Buttigieg.
“To compare Secretary Duffy’s record – which includes securing a $12.5 billion downpayment to begin updating our country’s air traffic control network after decades of neglect and launching a successful gamer campaign to supercharge ATC hiring – to a failed political hack like Pete Buttigieg is laughable.”
When asked by CNN to comment on Duffy’s criticisms, a spokesperson for Buttigieg pointed to a social media post on Monday, in which Buttigieg cited his own record, saying, “As secretary, I made sure to leave air travel in better condition than when we arrived. We reversed a decade of decline in air traffic controller staffing, drove down runway safety incidents, and when I left office we were experiencing the lowest flight cancellation rates in years.”
Duffy’s own congressional record on FAA funding is mixed.
In January 2019, during the government shutdown, Duffy joined 179 other Republicans in voting against a Democratic-backed spending bill aimed at reopening transportation and housing agencies. The legislation included funding for FAA operations and air traffic control modernization, along with numerous provisions unrelated to aviation.
But Duffy also voted for FAA funding and reauthorization measures in 2012 , 2013 and 2018 . A 2025 PolitiFact review found no public statements from Duffy at the time explaining his opposition to the 2019 bill. When asked about the vote six years later, a Duffy spokesperson told PolitiFact the legislation would have provided only a small increase in FAA funding.
A review of available archived pages from Duffy’s congressional website found no statements addressing national air traffic control modernization or FAA appropriations, with the FAA-related announcements identified in the review focusing on federal grants for airports in his Wisconsin district.
A separate search of Duffy’s appearances in the Internet Archive’s television news archive identified no discussions of FAA modernization before his criticism of Buttigieg following the January 2023 ground stop.
Duffy’s criticism of Buttigieg for taking time away from the job after his children were born also comes after Duffy spent part of his first two years as transportation secretary participating in a reality series with his own family.
Duffy and his wife, Rachel Campos-Duffy, and their nine children filmed “The Great American Road Trip” over a seven-month period, according to CNN’s previous reporting. The six-episode series, released on the Department of Transportation’s YouTube channel in August, followed the family through seven states as part of an effort to promote travel for the nation’s 250th anniversary.
A spokesperson for the Department of the Transportation defended Duffy’s participation in the series saying, “The series was filmed over the course of many months in small, one day or two stops.”
This story has been updated.

articles.title_orig: WhatsApp starts rolling out built-in cloud backup on Android, and it’s free
articles.title_zh: WhatsApp starts rolling out built-in cloud backup on Android, and it’s free
articles.content_orig:
Meta’s WhatsApp is making a huge change to chat backups, with a new built-in cloud backup option on Android that doesn’t rely on Google, and is free.
Spotted by WABetaInfo , WhatsApp for Android is adding its own cloud backup option. Prior to this, the app relied on Google Drive backup for transferring chats between devices or keeping a backup in case of accidental deletion.
“WhatsApp cloud storage” is showing up in the WhatsApp for Android v2.26.46.4 beta update, rolling out now, and includes 2GB of free storage for cloud backups. Everything is still end-to-end encrypted. Beyond the first 2GB, WhatsApp Plus ($2.99/month) adds 100GB, and Meta One ($7.99/month+) offers up to 4TB of cloud storage. WhatsApp will keep your backup for at least 4 months after the subscription ends, even if you are over the 2GB gap.
You can still choose to use Google Drive backups instead of the built-in option, but those using devices without a Google account or who are running low on Google storage may appreciate the option to switch.
It’s unclear exactly when this will be available to all WhatsApp users.
