articles.title_orig: Take-Two lays off Firaxis employees on eve of Grand Theft Auto VI launch
articles.title_zh: Take-Two lays off Firaxis employees on eve of Grand Theft Auto VI launch
articles.content_orig:
Firaxis, a sibling studio to Take-Two's Rockstar Games, is known for games like Sid Meier's Civilization VII and Marvel's Midnight Suns.
Take-Two Interactive is laying off employees at Firaxis Games, developer of Sid Meier's Civilization, Marvel's Midnight Suns , and the XCOM series. These layoffs at the Hunt Valley, MD-based studio come right before Take-Two's launch of Grand Theft Auto VI from subsidiary studio Rockstar Games and days after T2 shared its Q2 financial results .
A spokesperson for 2K, the Take-Two subsidiary that houses Firaxis, confirmed the layoffs in a statement to GameDeveloper.com. "Firaxis is restructuring and recentering around the studio’s core strength—designing world class strategy games that have set the industry standard for the genre for the last 30 years," they said.
"As part of these changes, the size of the studio is being reduced to focus on design, technology, and the player experience, which means saying goodbye to talented colleagues who helped build Firaxis. These decisions are never easy, but they’re essential to build the next chapter of Firaxis."
Related: 'It's common for there to be speculation and headlines:' Unity exec addresses acquisition rumors
The spokesperson also disclosed that Firaxis head Heather Hazen is leaving the company. "With the studio entering this reset, she feels this is the right, deliberate moment to hand over the reins to ensure the next studio leader has full ownership of this new era from the start. "
"This is a hard day, but it’s a necessary one for the health and future of our studio, our game franchises and our fans who deserve the very best. We are deeply grateful for the contributions every member of the team has made."

articles.title_orig: California DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after series of traffic incidents
articles.title_zh: California DMV bans Waymos from operating on state freeways after series of traffic incidents
articles.content_orig:
Some of the incidents reportedly involve Waymos in active construction zones.
The California Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) has ordered Waymo to stop operating its autonomous vehicles on California freeways, citing concerns that the vehicles pose an imminent public safety hazard.
The DMV's decision follows a series of incidents involving Waymo vehicles on Bay Area freeways, specifically citing two of them.
One of the incidents noted by the agency involved three Waymo vehicles that entered an active construction zone on U.S. Highway 101 near Burlingame, putting workers, equipment and other vehicles at risk. According to the DMV, similar incidents have occurred multiple times.
The other incident cited by the DMV drew additional attention after video showed a Waymo vehicle attempting to pass California Highway Patrol patrol cars conducting a traffic break on Interstate 280 earlier this month.
In a statement, Waymo said safety remains its top priority.
"Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations," a spokesperson told our sister station in the Bay Area.
SEE ALSO: California passenger stuck inside self-driving Waymo car through construction zone, followed by police
The DMV said concerns about Waymo vehicles on freeways are not new.
This is the second time this year Waymo has faced freeway restrictions. In May 2026, Waymo said it was pausing freeway operations in several cities, including San Francisco and Los Angeles, to improve how its vehicles respond in construction zones.
The California DMV says the new restrictions went into effect on Nov. 11 and "will remain in place until Waymo demonstrates to the department that it has taken effective corrective actions..."
"I see this as an opportunity to continue improving a technology," said Billy Riggs, a professor at the University of San Francisco.
Riggs said data shows autonomous vehicles remain safer than human drivers overall, but added that challenges are expected as the technology continues to develop.
"An automated vehicle can understand and identify all the aspects of the roadway and make really sophisticated judgments on them. But, many times, it can't understand context," Riggs said.
Earlier this year, San Francisco resident Elliot Slade said he was riding in a Waymo vehicle when it went off course and entered a construction zone. KGO-TV, our sister station in the Bay Area, previously spoke with Slade about the incident and interviewed him again on Monday.
"I used to use it all the time, and now it's like, eh, I'll walk or I'll take the (bus)," Slade said.
Slade said the experience left him skeptical about using Waymo vehicles in the future. While he acknowledged that accidents can happen with any vehicle, he said he remains concerned about the potential consequences if similar incidents continue.
"You had one chance to fix it if it went viral. And if they haven't made sure it's completely safe, then I'm disappointed. Super disappointed," Slade said.

articles.title_orig: Apple services, including iCloud, App Store, Apple Music, and more, hit by outage
articles.title_zh: Apple services, including iCloud, App Store, Apple Music, and more, hit by outage
articles.content_orig:
After a recent slew of tech outages, service disruptions, and flight chaos this week, it’s now Apple customers who are facing technical issues.
The iPhone maker’s System Status page indicates that there are issues with iCloud’s Account & Sign In services affecting “all users,” which could make the service slow or unavailable. The App Store, AppleCare on Device, and Apple Music are also experiencing issues, the page indicates.
Like all major tech companies, Apple faces outages and other technical issues affecting its cloud services at times. However, today’s issues are likely more noticeable to end users because problems with iCloud can lead to account sign-in problems. This could cause your iPhone to ask for your Apple ID and password, and you could see other attempts to sign in to services with your Apple account information fail.
On Reddit, some folks also noted that they were unable to activate a new iPhone , which is likely related to these ongoing issues.
Given the recent increase in AI-driven cyberattacks, users across social media have already begun to speculate about the cause. In particular, users are expressing concerns about the Apple outage, as it arrives only days after technical failures at Microsoft led to its cloud systems that power flagship services like Outlook and Teams failing due to cascading software issues .
Similarly, a brief outage of Chase’s banking app this week garnered attention, as did an ongoing partial outage (at the time of publication) of the National Security Agency’s internal classified network, both of which were blamed on software glitches.
So far, none of the outages in the past week have been attributed to cyberattacks, but rather to technical problems.
Apple responded to TechCrunch’s request for comment (which it initially gave to Bloomberg ), noting that the outages were caused by an internal update and not a cyberattack. “Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible,” the statement read.
After the initial outages were reported, Apple’s status page was updated to include other outages impacting Apple School Manager, iCloud Mail, iCloud Web Apps (iCloud.com),  Schoolwork, and the Volume Purchase Program.
By 6 PM ET on Tuesday, the status page showed all the outages were resolved.

articles.content_orig:

The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17).
That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement.
"While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update .
The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt.
The new rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff.
On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security launches with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.)
That work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA said in an Oct. 28 update . And those tweaks apparently worked.
"All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the company wrote in today's update.
Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added.
Vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin . Today's update did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun.
If that investigation finds a serious issue with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is currently recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28 .)
NASA plans to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that launches Artemis astronauts to space. So the fact that the Centaur performed nominally on Sunday is a bit of good news for the space agency.
Vulcan's grounding is a big deal, no matter what the anomaly investigation ends up finding. The U.S. doesn't have a surfeit of powerful rockets, after all, and two of them — Vulcan and New Glenn — are out of commission at the moment.
There's considerable pressure on both Vulcan and New Glenn to bounce back strong, for the nation faces an impending launch crunch in the next few years. SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets and shift its launch load over to the fully reusable Starship megarocket. SpaceX is expected to prioritize its own needs in Starship's early days, using the vehicle primarily to build out its next-gen Starlink broadband constellation and Starmind AI data center network.
The Vulcan failure also impacts Amazon — specifically, the company's plan to build out Amazon Leo, which will compete with SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon has booked about 100 launches on a variety of rockets to build its constellation, which will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Thirty-eight of those bookings are for Vulcan; Sunday's launch was the first of those.
The other rockets Amazon has booked are the Atlas V, New Glenn, Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6 . About 400 operational Amazon Leo satellites have reached orbit to date across 14 launches (not including Sunday's failure).
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

articles.title_orig: Apple, Google and more services down in latest wave of widespread outages
articles.title_zh: Apple, Google and more services down in latest wave of widespread outages
articles.content_orig:
Apple said it was experiencing tech issues Tuesday that were affecting several of its popular consumer-facing services.
As of 2 p.m. ET, Apple’s own system status page showed that Apple Business, Apple School Manager, AppleCare, iCloud Mail and Web Apps, and SchoolWork were each experiencing outages.
Stream Philadelphia News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC10.
Earlier, the page showed the App Store and Apple Music experiencied outages.
“Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning,” an Apple spokesperson told NBC News. “We’re working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible.”
At Apple stores in New York and Chicago, employees told NBC News earlier in the day that their internal software had stopped working and they had been unable to complete purchases or make appointments.
Marriott International, the largest U.S. hotel operator, was also having technology issues that guests reported had impacted reservations and check-ins, among other problems, according to users posting on Reddit. Downdetector.com also reported that Marriott was experiencing an outage.
Marriott, which has 10,200 properties and more than 1.8 million rooms under its corporate umbrella, did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Associated Press.
Gmail also appeared to experience an outage briefly Tuesday, with some users reporting issues accessing their email, according to Downdetector. The issue did not appear to be widespread and the company posted on X that they weren't "currently seeing evidence of a broad Gmail service disruption."
The outages come on the heels of a string of major disruptions impacting U.S. services over the past several days — including Monday's Chase, Bank of America and Wells Fargo banking disruptions and United Airlines departing-flight system glitch , following Friday's nationwide FAA ground stop and Thursday's Microsoft cloud outage.
President Donald Trump brushed off the recent outages that wreaked havoc on air travel, banks and emails, saying Tuesday, “it’s life.”
“It’s life, it’s life,” he told reporters during his trip to the Philippines when asked about the outages. “When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”
While none of the issues appear to be related, they’ve exposed America’s reliance on older infrastructure and revealed the extent to which companies and governments are being forced to upgrade systems in the AI age. The incidents have also stoked unfounded paranoia that something larger may be afoot.

articles.title_orig: What to know about the online banking delays that affected major US banks
articles.title_zh: What to know about the online banking delays that affected major US banks
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of Chase Bank customers reported they had trouble using their online accounts on Monday.
“JPMorganChase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug,” a spokesperson said Monday. “It is taking longer than usual to service some customers.”
The Chase spokesperson went on to say it was a “bug,” rather than a widespread cyberattack.
Social media users reported issues with transactions at physical Chase branches, as well, and some local bank branches told customers earlier in the day that they were having issues with their internal system. However, Chase said in a statement that “customers still have access to their accounts and funds.”
The outage wasn’t caused by a cloud-related issue or a cyber attack, a source familiar with the matter told CNN. Rather, an update on the company’s own physical computer systems inadvertently caused issues.
As of 2:00 p.m. ET, more than 4,700 customers reported issues with Chase, according to Downdetector.
Customers reported issues at other major banks, including Bank of America, Wells Fargo, and U.S. Bank, though on a smaller scale.
The reports with the other banks appear to be related to sending money through Zelle, a digital payment network, to Chase accounts.
“U.S. Bank systems are not directly impacted. However, clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays,” U.S. Bank said in a statement.
Bank of America also said it was operating normally on Monday.
“Clients experiencing delays with other providers may wish to contact them directly for the latest information,” a spokesperson told CNN.
Zelle said that its service is “operating as it should.” The money-transferring service is owned by a consortium of US banks called Early Warning Services, and Zelle said it does not hold consumer funds.
“An issue at the financial institutions may be impacting broader services, including Zelle payments, for some of their customers,” a Zelle spokesperson said.
Chase also said it wasn’t a systemic issue.
“Other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,” the spokesperson continued.
Monday’s Chase outage marked the third straight weekday with a massive technical failure.
On Thursday, a Microsoft outage cut off email access to millions of people across 74 countries and territories. On Friday, a Federal Aviation Administration systems failure led to a nationwide ground stop .
And on Monday afternoon, United Airlines reported a systemwide computer problem that delayed flights.
The incidents don’t share the same scope or root causes. Microsoft blamed a Windows defect, a traffic overload and capacity constraints. The FAA cited a router deployment issue and excessive data flooding its systems. It’s not yet clear what caused the Chase or United outages on Monday.
But the glitches share a common theme: “the complexity and fragility of the systems that we depend on every day,” Mike Chapple, a professor of IT, Analytics, and Operations at the University of Notre Dame, said in emailed comments.
“In each of these cases, what started as an issue in one small part of a larger system quickly spread, causing massive disruptions nationwide,” he added.
Complexity and interdependence aren’t inherently flaws — in fact, they make systems more resilient, noted Rebecca Krauthamer, CEO and cofounder of QuSecure, a cryptography provider for the US government.
“But when dependencies on systems aren’t sufficiently understood, failures can cascade across institutions and industries,” she added.
Think about it like the Titanic: The watertight bulkheads were unable to withstand a failure that exceeded the ship’s architects’ worst-case-scenario assumptions. Even the best-designed systems sometimes succumb to threats and problems that the designers couldn’t have imagined when they built them.
The problem with interdependent technology systems is that system failures are rarely isolated incidents: Our heavy reliance on a handful of systems means failures have tended to bring down systems across the world.
“The question for leaders is not whether one system will fail but how many other things fail with it, and how fast you can contain it,” said Madhu Shashanka, founder of Concentric AI.
This story has been updated with additional developments.
CNN’s David Goldman contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.title_zh: UK sanctions firms over Israeli West Bank settlements
articles.content_orig:
Foreign affairs minister Penny Wong says rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are ‘extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution’
Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast
Australia has announced another tranche of sanctions on individuals and organisations involved in illegal settlement expansion and human rights abuses against Palestinians in the West Bank .
In a statement, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong , said it was the first time Australian sanctions had targeted a construction company involved in the building of settlements.
The sanctions prohibit Australians and Australian businesses from trading with or providing financial or other support to three individuals and four organisations.
“We are taking these actions because the rapid expansion of settlements and settler violence are extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution,” Wong’s statement said.
“This includes the E1 settlement where demolitions and the displacement of Palestinians have occurred in recent weeks. Israeli settlements in the West Bank are illegal under international law.”
Among those sanctioned is Daniella Weiss and her Israeli settler organisation, the Nachala movement, which the government said has provided support for outposts and settlements that have perpetrated serious human rights abuses.
Weiss is known as the “godmother” of the settler movement and was sanctioned by the UK in May 2025, shortly after she appeared on a Louis Theroux’s documentary The Settlers .
Prominent West Bank settler Eliav Libi has also been sanctioned, as well as the Eyal Hari Yehuda construction company which has helped develop settlements and outposts and demolished Palestinian structures in the West Bank.
Wong said the sanctioned individuals and organisations had “actively participated in the planning, coordination and establishment of new settlements, including raising funds, recruitment of volunteers and providing support to violent settlers”.
Speaking on ABC radio on Wednesday morning, Wong said Australia had been coordinating with the UK on the sanctions.
“We thought it was very important to work with the United Kingdom to have a coordinated set of sanctions ahead of those decisions.
“We urge Israel to desist from proceeding with this settlement, which renders likely unviable the prospect of a Palestinian state.”
Wong said she had spoken to her Israeli counterpart, Gideon Sa’ar, on Tuesday night when she “outlined” Australia’s position.
“We’ve made clear we will continue to take action in respect of those involved in the settlement enterprise. The settlement enterprise is violent.”
after newsletter promotion
Wong had signalled further sanctions in September, after the government ruled out an import ban on trade from illegal settlements in the West Bank.
On Wednesday, the foreign affairs minister said the government was still considering further action, but provided no detail.
“We’ll continue to look at targeted measures we can take to push back against what the current Israeli government is doing,” Wong told journalists.
When asked whether Wong was concerned Israel would respond to Australia sanctions with countermeasures, the minister said it had in the past.
“We’ve seen the Israeli government take action against Australia, including asking our diplomats to leave Ramallah. We’ve also seen the caretaker prime minister, Netanyahu, be very public in his criticism of Australia.
“So obviously, there is a reaction to Australia acting, but we think this is the right thing to do.”
The statement warned Australian businesses they must not bid for construction tenders for illegal settlement developments.
Individuals breaching sanctions can attract a penalty of up to 10 years’ imprisonment and a fine of up to $910,000 or three times the value of the relevant transaction.
Businesses can be fined up to $3.64m or three times the value of the relevant transaction.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI sued by California after admitting to 80 loss-of-control incidents
articles.title_zh: OpenAI sued by California after admitting to 80 loss-of-control incidents
articles.content_orig:
California sued OpenAI yesterday, alleging it has tried to evade responsibility for the Hugging Face attack and about 80 other incidents in which the company lost control of its AI. The lawsuit was filed under the state’s public nuisance and unfair competition laws.
The July 2026 hack of Hugging Face and other attacks carried out by OpenAI’s autonomous agents “may just be the tip of the iceberg,” said a lawsuit filed in a state court by California Attorney General Rob Bonta. “OpenAI recently admitted to the Attorney General’s Office that it has lost control of its autonomous AI agents over 80 times during testing.”
OpenAI had publicly reported only 27 such incidents, showing that “OpenAI’s public reports do not represent the full scope of loss-of-control incidents involving OpenAI’s models that have impacted third parties,” the lawsuit said. OpenAI “knowingly tested a dangerous product without proper oversight or safety procedures and misled the public about it,” Bonta said in a press release .
OpenAI models are “able to find novel vulnerabilities in computer networks, quickly break down defenses, and autonomously carry out cyberattacks,” Bonta’s lawsuit said. OpenAI puts safeguards in its publicly released models to prevent this behavior, “but deliberately omits or removes these protections while experimenting with and training its models,” the lawsuit said.
In the attack on Hugging Face, OpenAI agents “employed complicated hacking methodologies and involved coordinated actions by hundreds of individual autonomous AI agents that should have been contained in OpenAI’s research environment,” the lawsuit said.
Known attacks “include unauthorized access of and cyberattacks on databases containing code that powers countless applications; informational websites that are trusted and valuable resources for the public; and foreign government databases storing sensitive health information,” the lawsuit said. “Swarms of OpenAI’s experimental AI agents have even compromised OpenAI’s own internal infrastructure, in an attack that managed to obtain administrator-level access to critical OpenAI systems.”
The lawsuit accused OpenAI of refusing to provide sufficient detail about the incidents. Bonta announced an investigation into OpenAI in early September and sent an investigative subpoena to the company with additional questions on September 30.
“Rather than take responsibility and be transparent with the public and with regulators so that these loss-of-control incidents can be analyzed and prevented, OpenAI thwarted the Attorney General’s efforts to investigate these incidents, including by refusing to provide detailed information about the full universe of incidents known to the company,” the lawsuit filed yesterday said.
OpenAI told Ars that most of the incidents identified in its review had low severity, and none matched the severity or scale of the Hugging Face attack. OpenAI defended its response to the California investigation, saying it provided multiple technical briefings to Bonta and his staff, answered the office’s questions, and offered more technical briefings to discuss its remediation efforts and plans for addressing the problems.
“Since the Hugging Face incident, we’ve undertaken an extensive and transparent effort to understand and address misaligned model activity,” OpenAI said. “We’ve published a detailed technical report, commissioned and published a separate independent report, notified affected organizations, strengthened safeguards across our research systems, and created a framework for additional identification and disclosure of misalignment. This lawsuit appears to single out OpenAI over a challenge that’s been identified by every major AI lab. We take misalignment seriously, and we have engaged—and will continue to engage—constructively with the attorney general’s office to share information and advance strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”
California’s lawsuit accuses OpenAI of creating a public nuisance as defined in state law, and several violations of the state’s Unfair Competition Law. Alleged violations include “causing and/or allowing agents to gain unauthorized access to third-party computer systems,” developing AI models without adequate security measures, and making false or misleading claims about the safety of its AI products.
California is seeking an injunction to stop the alleged violations of the Unfair Competition Law and to require civil penalties and financial damages. It also wants an order to “compel OpenAI to abate the ongoing public nuisance their conduct has created in California.” Bonta said in his press release that “the Hugging Face attack was the predictable result of an internal culture at OpenAI that prioritizes growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability—and this was only one of 80 known incidents.”
OpenAI was sued in September by Legal Advocates for Safe Science & Technology (LASST), a nonprofit that alleged violations of California’s Unfair Competition Law and the state’s Comprehensive Computer Data Access and Fraud Act. “OpenAI and frontier AI developers more broadly can’t avoid the consequences of their unsafe actions just by claiming that ‘an AI did it,’” the group said. “Autonomous AI agents will continue to hack, steal data, disrupt systems, and violate rights until a court steps in.”
OpenAI said in response to the LASST lawsuit that “Hugging Face was a serious incident and we’ve taken a series of actions in response to it, but this lawsuit is completely without merit.”

articles.title_orig: GTA 6: How one school is battling the 'GTA flu' with warnings to parents and prizes for pupils
articles.title_zh: GTA 6: How one school is battling the 'GTA flu' with warnings to parents and prizes for pupils
articles.content_orig:
My husband and I already know we want to play Grand Theft Auto 6 together. What we don't know is when.
The game comes out November 19. Right now, our controllers are under a pile of burp cloths, and every time our daughter toddles past the TV, someone hits pause so she doesn't see what we're playing.
We met in a game, and for years gaming was how we spent our time together, 20-plus hours a week. Then, last year, we became first-time parents. Now we have two problems we never expected: finding time to play and figuring out what's OK to play when a 15-month-old is watching.
Before I met my husband, gaming was something I did alone. It was how I unwound after work.
Then a random Halo Infinite lobby put us on the same team. I'd like to say it was love at first sight, but it was really love at first aim-down-sights. One match turned into two, and then our after-work matches became a regular nightly duo, and a duo turned into a relationship.
For years, gaming was our date night, our downtime, and our shared language : 30-plus hours a week, side by side.
When I got pregnant, we didn't stop playing. We just changed how we played. We still logged about 20 hours a week, often passing one controller back and forth through open-world single-player titles while the baby kicked to remind us she was on her way.
After our daughter was born, we gamed for exactly zero hours. As she got older, we started finding our way back. First came quick multiplayer matches in Halo Infinite that we could drop at a moment's notice. Then we started playing the campaign of the recently remastered Halo: Combat Evolved together, very slowly, with long breaks between sessions because one of us always got pulled away by a suspiciously quiet toddler all of a sudden.
Those big open-world games we love didn't survive that schedule. My husband played all of Starfield while I slept. Or "slept," since most nights I was half-awake in a haze of revenge bedtime procrastination, doomscrolling long past when I should have closed my eyes. Cyberpunk 2077 is still sitting in our backlog.
Add BI in Google so our reporting is easier to find when you’re searching for what matters.
Now GTA 6 is looming, bigger than all of them, and that's the part that worries me, but we're more determined than ever to try. She's almost a year and a half now, and we want back the pastime that brought us together in the first place. What better way to celebrate our original duo than by playing as a couple in the biggest game of the year?
The first time it hit me, I was sneaking in some Fallout 4 next to my husband on the couch. I was clearing out a raider camp, with gunfire cracking and limbs flying, when I landed a shot that took a raider's head clean off. Out of the corner of my eye, I saw my daughter's little head snap toward the TV. The sound had pulled her in, and she was staring right at the screen as the body hit the ground.
I froze. I'd played violent games for years without a second thought, and I'd even started gaming again when she was barely mobile and hardly noticed anything, and somewhere along the way she'd started to watch. Keeping up with how fast she was changing and rethinking my habits with every new leap she made had already had my head spinning. Now here was one more thing I'd missed.
Now we feel pulled in two directions. We want to protect her from anything overly graphic, and we still love the games we've always played, which aren't exactly gentle.
So we've started treating game settings like childproofing. We look for options that reduce or turn off blood and gore, or change the color of blood. We turn the volume down so gunfire doesn't startle her, and we play with subtitles, or one of us wears headphones. We look for settings that tone down bright flashes to protect her eyes.
I'll be checking GTA 6 's menu for every one of these on day one. And honestly, a lot of these accessibility settings make the game better for me, too.
We don't have it all figured out, but we have a plan. Violent missions wait until she's asleep. Naps are now prime gaming time. And when we can't both have a controller, we'll go back to what got us through pregnancy: passing one back and forth.
It feels right that GTA 6 stars Jason and Lucia, a couple who do everything as a team. They just have fewer diapers to change.
We may not reach the end credits on launch week, or even launch month, but we'll get there together, one nap at a time.

articles.title_orig: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines
articles.title_zh: The data is very preliminary, but Vulcan failure may not be due to BE-4 engines
articles.content_orig:
United Launch Alliance (ULA) confirmed Tuesday morning that its return-to-flight launch of the Vulcan rocket began failing during the initial stages of the mission.
“While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff, the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit,” the company said .
The launch company also confirmed reporting by Ars that the Centaur V upper stage and the solid rocket boosters performed nominally during the flight.
Critically, ULA did not provide any specific information about the “low booster performance.” This matters greatly because the core stage of the Vulcan rocket is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are provided by Blue Origin. That company’s own New Glenn rocket uses a similar but slightly more powerful version of the BE-4 engine. And New Glenn experienced its own catastrophic failure in May during a ground test, a failure that later was attributed to a main oxygen valve on one of the BE-4 engines.
Information about the Vulcan failure is being closely held by ULA and Blue Origin, who have only acknowledged that they’re working together to investigate the cause. According to two sources, the investigation is “incredibly complicated” and remains in the early stages.
However, according to preliminary data, two independent sources indicated to Ars that the problem is currently believed to have originated on the launch vehicle side rather than in the engines themselves. The issue may be related to systems that feed methane and liquid oxygen propellant to the engines.
ULA engineers are looking at the possibility that one of the two BE-4 engines started producing lower thrust shortly after liftoff and never ramped back up to full throttle for the remainder of the burn. Video observations from high-zoom tracking cameras appeared to show one engine slightly dimmer than the other after Vulcan jettisoned its solid rocket boosters nearly two minutes into flight. An asymmetric shutdown of the BE-4 engines could also have contributed to the sudden attitude motion indicated by ULA’s telemetry-driven real-time animation near stage separation.
The Federal Aviation Administration is overseeing the investigation, which is being led by ULA. Again, this information is preliminary, and no definitive conclusions can or should be drawn.
This was the fifth flight of the Vulcan rocket since its debut in January 2024. Two of the previous flights have experienced issues with the nozzles on its solid rocket boosters, but in both cases, the rocket was able to compensate for the reduced and asymmetric thrust and reach its intended orbit. The second nozzle issue caused Vulcan to stand down for nine months.
This latest setback is likely to sideline Vulcan for at least half a year, and probably longer. Most impacted will be the US Space Force, which has national security payloads waiting for a ride to space on Vulcan, and Amazon, which had more than a dozen launches of its Amazon Leo constellation on the manifest for 2027. It would exacerbate a worsening launch crisis in the United States.
There are potentially serious implications for Blue Origin as well, which is seeking to return New Glenn to flight as early as January. Last Tuesday, the company said a modified BE-4 main oxygen valve had successfully completed qualification testing.
“Our modified valve has already been incorporated into engines slated for upcoming flights, and we are now rolling it out across the remaining fleet,” the company said . “We expect to complete the anomaly investigation later this month.”
If Vulcan’s failure were ultimately due to a problem with the BE-4 engine, it would certainly delay the New Glenn rocket’s return to flight. This would be a setback not just for Blue Origin but for NASA, which is counting on the super heavy lift rocket to do much of the heavy lifting for its Artemis Program and Moon Base.

articles.title_orig: Is Apple down? Thousands report problems accessing services
articles.title_zh: Is Apple down? Thousands report problems accessing services
articles.content_orig:
Apple said an internal update was to blame for a major outage on Nov. 17 that hit its App Store, iCloud, Apple Pay and other software, with thousands of users reporting problems online.
In a statement to USA TODAY, Apple said it was working to fix the affected systems, and services are expected to return to normal soon.
"Many of our systems are back up and running after an internal update caused some outages this morning. We're working to get the remaining systems online as soon as possible," the company said.
Apple, on its System Status page , confirmed outages on App Store, Apple Music and AppleCare on Device, as well as issues with iCloud Account & Sign In. The company told Bloomberg the problems weren't caused by a cyberattack.
According to outage tracker Downdetector, reports of issues with Apple Pay began to spike at around 11:40 a.m. ET with a peak of reports at around 12:15 p.m. ET. Outage reports for iCloud also started to surge just before noon ET, though reports on Downdetector don't reflect every user experiencing a problem. Those reports had dropped significantly by mid-afternoon.
The Apple software issues came on the heels of a major banking outage on Nov. 16 that stemmed from Chase Bank. It also impacted Wells Fargo, Bank of America, online payment platform Zelle and other institutions.
Last week, a communications outage disrupted air traffic across the United States, and a Microsoft outage prevented many from checking their Outlook email and accessing Microsoft 365 services like Teams and Word.

articles.title_zh: Outage math at the airport: When a four-hour Uber beats waiting out a ground stop
articles.content_orig:
By MELISSA KOENIG, US REPORTER and ASSOCIATED PRESS
Published: 17:12 EST, 16 November 2026 | Updated: 08:04 EST, 17 November 2026
United Airlines flights across the United States were grounded on Monday night, just days after a technical issue prompted the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to ground all flights nationwide.
The airline announced on social media that it was experiencing a 'widespread system outage' as it apologized to customers 'for the inconvenience.'
'We're aware of the widespread system and our teams are working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible,' it posted on X.
'We appreciate your patience while we work through this,' the airline added, urging anyone with scheduled flights to keep checking their flight status on the app.
The post has since been deleted, as a spokesperson for the airline told the Daily Mail that the issue has been resolved.
'While some flights were delayed, there was no impact on flights in progress, or on United Express flights,' the spokesperson said, adding: 'There is no indication that this was a cybersecurity-related issue.'
The update came after frustrated travelers took to social media to bemoan how their flights could not take off.
'Currently stuck on the tarmac,' one X user posted, blaming it on an IT issue in which the airline 'can't clear planes for takeoff as [they] can't connect to the weight system.'
United Airlines flights across the country were grounded Monday night as the airline experienced a 'widespread system outage'
The issue comes just days after a technical issue prompted the Federal Aviation Administration to ground all flights nationwide
United Airlines said on social media its teams were 'working hard to get things back up and running as soon as possible'
The outage is now the latest in a string of technical issues that have crippled businesses around the country and left airline passengers stranded for hours amid a rare nationwide ground stop.
Earlier Monday, thousands of customers with Chase, Bank of America, Capital One and Wells Fargo also flagged being unable to log in or transfer money , according to Down Detector, a website which tracks real-time user reports.
A spokesperson for Chase told the Daily Mail the outage was caused by a technical bug.
'Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds,' they said. 'We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible.'
Chase also addressed one complaint on X, telling a client: 'I do apologize, it appears that we are currently working to resolve an issue with online banking.
'Please try again at a later time. We're sorry for any inconvenience, and appreciate your patience.'
Wells Fargo also posted a note on its website telling customers that 'online banking isn't available right now' due to 'technical issues'.
A spokesperson for Chase later noted that the technical problems were not the result of a cyberattack.
'JPMorgan Chase has experienced a temporary issue related to a software bug in an on-premise hardware system - it is not cyber-related,' said spokesman Joe Evangelisti.
In the same statement, Evangelisti said that this was a Chase-only issue.
'This is not a systemic issue - other banks may have been impacted by slowness in transactions only to the extent that they were a party to a transaction with us,' he said.
Customers at three major US banks have been locked out of their accounts as Chase and Wells Fargo all experienced outages on Monday afternoon
Over 20,000 flights were canceled from Friday to Sunday, according to airline tracker FlightAware. During that same period, over 25,000 flights were delayed, and lingering impacts have bled into Monday
A spokesman for US Bank said its systems were not directly impacted but that 'clients attempting to send or receive Zelle payments with another financial institution may experience transaction delays.'
Zelle is the peer-to-peer payment system that major US banks use to allow customers to send money to friends and family at near-instant speed.
It is owned by Arizona-based Early Warning Services, which in turn is owned by financial institutions including Bank of America, Capital One, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, Truist, US Bank and Wells Fargo.
A spokesman for Early Warning Services said the Zelle network was fully operational.
'An issue at the financial institutions may be delaying Zelle payments for some of their customers,' the spokesman said.
Still, the outage sparked panic as it came just three days after Microsoft experienced widespread issues on Friday , leaving people unable to access Outlook, Teams and Copilot applications.
Businesses ground to a halt, healthcare providers lost contact with patients, courts lost live feeds, and governments struggled to communicate.
The suspected cause was a faulty network configuration change that resulted in numerous servers becoming unavailable, overloading the remaining infrastructure.
The FAA also issued a rare nationwide ground stop at all US airports following a major communications failure on Friday.
'What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,' Trump said on Monday of the FAA outage that forced thousands of cancelled and delayed flights over the weekend
The Air Traffic Control System Command Center (ATCSCC) said on Friday that the  halting of 3,500 US flights for five hours was 'due to extraordinary circumstances for safety reasons'.
'There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution, all flights have been halted,' the FAA said.
'Every flight has been accounted for, and international flights will be handled on a case-by-case basis.'
President Donald Trump has since blamed half-century-old aviation equipment for the ground stop, which led to thousands of cancellations and travel woes for over a million passengers.
'We have old, broken equipment,' the President said Monday at the White House before departing for his trip to Asia on board the new Air Force One plane gifted to the administration by Qatari officials.
He noted that some of the equipment that went down was 55 years old.
'We essentially want to blow it up and put new in, and we can do it simultaneously with very little trouble. What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack.'
The incident marked only the second time since the 9/11 terrorist attacks that a nationwide ground stop was implemented.
The stoppage also prevented any domestic flights from taking off, resulting in one of the worst travel snarls in recent US history. It began around 3.30pm and was not lifted until around 8.20pm.
More than 20,000 flights were canceled from Friday to Sunday, according to airline tracker FlightAware. During that same period, over 25,000 flights were delayed, and lingering impacts have bled into Monday.
It is estimated that more than one million American travelers have been impacted by the outage.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy claimed Biden-era upgrades were shoddy
The President also cast blame on his predecessor for the FAA glitch.
'The Biden administration hooked up a lot of copper into glass. And copper, if you know anything about electrical engineering, you cannot hook up copper into glass. So a lot of money was wasted, but the equipment is very old,' Trump said.
He was referring to Biden-era upgrades to communication systems built on copper wiring that were upgraded to fiber-optic, or glass, wires.
Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said the upgrade work was shoddy, resulting in the outage.
Trump said the upgrade was a waste of money and more cash would be needed from Congress to fully upgrade the system and prevent future issues.
'We want to make it beyond safe. We want to have the best system in the world, and for that we need Congress,' the President told reporters.

articles.title_orig: Three China-related Items to Consider as Trump Again Meets with Xi
articles.title_zh: Three China-related Items to Consider as Trump Again Meets with Xi
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.
Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine . And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week,  teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”
U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
Trump’s break from long-standing tradition in U.S.-Russia relations was real, but it should not have been entirely surprising.
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.
The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.
The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.
The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink , the satellite internet service owned by Musk.
Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.
The summit’s stark lack of substance surprised even the closest China watchers.
Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta Conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide , demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.
And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

articles.title_orig: Social media algorithms are encouraging Americans to freak out about the tech outages
articles.title_zh: Social media algorithms are encouraging Americans to freak out about the tech outages
articles.content_orig:
By PHILLIP NIETO, US POLITICAL REPORTER
Published: 09:27 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 14:17 EST, 17 November 2026
JD Vance has told Americans they do not need a bunker or a food stockpile, days after a global email collapse, a nationwide ground stop and a banking meltdown.
‘A lot of my friends have reached out asking if they should prepare to build a bunker or stock up on food and water,’ the vice president told Fox News host Laura Ingraham on Monday night.
‘We don’t see a crisis coming down,’ Vance added, ‘but you have to be prepared for everything.’
‘We want to make sure we prevent the worst outcomes, but we’re also prepared for the worst outcomes,’ he continued.
Ingraham had asked him point blank whether Americans should be prepping for a major global catastrophe. It comes after Britain and France have told their own citizens to keep days of food and water at home.
Vance brushed off the reporting behind the question, including accounts of Pentagon bases preparing to run off the grid for 90 days, as ‘just basic good government, making sure that our military is prepared, God forbid, if there was a crisis.’
Meanwhile, Google has warned corporate America that hackers powered by artificial intelligence are running autonomous attacks across major systems.
The company's report released on Monday claims these AI hackers can constantly work around security patches, write working exploits and fire them at online servers.
Vance has told Americans they do not need a bunker or a food stockpile, days after a global email collapse, a nationwide ground stop and a banking meltdown
Google has warned corporate America that hackers powered by artificial intelligence are now running autonomous attacks across major systems
Tens of thousands of travelers were left stranded over the weekend after the FAA issued a nationwide grounding for all flights
Google drew no connection between its findings and last week’s failures, and federal officials say they have found no evidence that anyone attacked anything.
Moreover, Hackers have compromised some of the world’s most visited websites in a sweeping cyberattack targeting users’ money and credit card details.
Security researchers identified malicious code in website tools used by 178 organizations, including Zoom, CNN, the BBC, HSBC, Equifax, Salesforce, Peacock, IKEA, Fox News, NPR, the ASPCA and Invisalign.
The attack, detected Monday evening, targeted Optimizely, a service companies use to test different website layouts and features.
Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and Copilot services collapsed on Thursday and stayed down for users in 74 countries into the weekend.
On Friday, approxiatemately 10,000 flights were disrupted after the Federal Aviation Administration halted departures across the country, the second nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has blamed a router that contractor L3Harris Technologies installed at a remote FAA radio site in Arkansas.
It flooded a network still running on equipment built in 2001 and scheduled for replacement in 2006.
Duffy called FBI Director Kash Patel to pull agents into the investigation, the router now sits in a laboratory in Florida, and the FAA has switched off the broadcast function on all 69 of the same devices across the national airspace.
By Monday, banks had been affected by the the outages as thousands of customers at Chase, Wells Fargo, US Bank, Capital One, Truist and Bank of America reporting they could not see their balances or move cash.
United Airlines also delayed its own departures that same afternoon when pilots lost the weight and balance figures they need to leave the gate, stopping hundreds of flights.

articles.title_orig: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
articles.title_zh: FAA pauses installation of new routers after ground stop
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to issue a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.
Tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.
The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.
The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.
Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.
"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety."
The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the issue and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.
The senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.
CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.
Duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.
Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, said Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.
"I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he said. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization."
Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.
— CNBC's Phil LeBeau , Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: A Kremlin trap? Europe sees danger in Vladimir Putin’s new demand in U.S. talks
articles.title_zh: A Kremlin trap? Europe sees danger in Vladimir Putin’s new demand in U.S. talks
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — When European nations said they wanted greater involvement in Ukraine peace talks , this was almost certainly not what they had in mind.
Europe has long demanded more say in negotiations to end Russia’s war , fearful of being frozen out by Washington and Moscow. They dread a deal favorable to President Vladimir Putin — who will meet President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping at a historic three-way meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday.
The good news for them is that the United States says it is now pushing to include Europe in the next rounds of diplomacy. The bad news, say governments, officials and foreign policy analysts, is the alarming new suggestion from Trump’s team: that the entire future of European security should be up for discussion too  — the same demand that Putin has pushed for years .
To the Russian leader, redrawing Europe’s security map means scaling back NATO’s presence, righting what he perceives as the injustices imposed on Moscow after the Soviet Union’s collapse. A succession of senior European officials have lambasted the idea, warning that Washington risks “walking into Moscow’s trap,” as Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s foreign policy chief, put it.
“This is all rather bizarre,” former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves said, summing up this sentiment in an interview with NBC News on Monday.
It’s not clear how or why the U.S. came to float a maximalist demand that Putin first made in 2021, one that was widely rejected by Western governments months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine . But in recent days, as Washington ups its pressure for a breakthrough in peace talks, Russia and the U.S. have both revived the idea.
Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law and envoy, wrote Friday that talks should tackle the “broader postwar European security arrangements.”
Earlier this month, he lamented “decades of mistrust” and “competing security concerns” between Russia and Europe, vowing to address these by building an “enduring framework for long-term European security and stability.” Kushner has also stressed that NATO would remain central to European defense and that no country should have a veto over another’s alliances.
Trump himself has also hinted that he seeks a final deal encompassing the entire continent. “It’s going to be a big agreement and it’s going to involve more than Ukraine,” he told reporters in the Oval Office earlier this month. “I could even say it might involve all of Europe. It’s going to be a big, beautiful agreement, and everyone’s going to be thrilled.”
Instead, the idea has been met with unease and dismay, viewed by many in Europe as echoing Putin’s hard-line war goals.
Whereas Kushner described Europe and Russia as neighbors unable to resolve their differences, the historical record shows the aggression has chiefly been directed one way. Russia seized Ukraine’s Crimean Peninsula in 2014, then launching a full-scale invasion in 2022, while waging sabotage, cyberattacks and disinformation against the West.
Kushner’s suggestion also touches on a central European fear: that Washington will pursue a deal at almost any cost, even if  that emboldens Putin to expand his aggression.
“Why are two real estate agents pushing this idea?” Ilves  said referring to Kushner and Steve Witkoff, another Trump envoy, both of whom made their fortunes in real estate before entering diplomacy.
“These people aren’t even diplomats,” said Ilves, who led his former Soviet republic from 2006 to 2016. “I’m not sure they have much of an idea of the long history of the development of security architecture in Europe relating to Russia.”
Asked about the criticisms, assistant White House press secretary Olivia Wales said the U.S. proposal sought to “strengthen existing European security arrangements, with NATO at their core, while developing practical mechanisms to prevent future conflict.”
Security guarantees for  Ukraine “cannot be designed without understanding the broader security framework in which they will operate,” she said in an email, adding that any final agreement must respect Europe and Ukraine’s sovereignty “and be agreed by the relevant parties.”
European officials are nonetheless unnerved by Kushner’s remarks.
Kallas, the E.U. foreign policy chief, described Russia’s maximalist war demands as “really absurd,” while German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul pointed out that “Europe has a security architecture — we don’t need a new one.”
Elsewhere, Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys said the rules were not the issue: “The problem is that Russia is breaking them.” And even Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney was adamant that the “security architecture for free Europe will be determined by free Europe and NATO, not by Russia.”
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the idea as “dangerous,” saying that European security “should not be the main agenda.”
Ukraine’s view is that Russia is in no place to make such demands, given that it’s spent more than four years failing to win the war.
“At this stage, the most Putin can negotiate is a fair ceasefire along the current line of contact,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said. And “frankly, Europe does not need a new security order; it already exists, and Russia is constantly violating it.”
Kyiv and its European backers also argue that a ceasefire must come before any peace talks, accusing Russia of stalling so it can keep bombing civilian infrastructure ahead of the frigid winter.
If Europe accepts Russia’s demands about wider continental security before there is a ceasefire, Moscow “will try to create the impression that it’s our fault that the war continues, because we don’t want to accept all their demands,” according to Sven Biscop, a director at the Egmont Institute, a Belgian think tank.
He said he believed dialogue with Russia is a good thing, a view echoed by influential Finnish President Alexander Stubb, who in an interview with the Financial Times published Tuesday said that it had been “irresponsible” to outsource talks with Putin to the U.S., which he said could be leaning toward carving up Europe into spheres of influence.
Back in Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., urged Trump’s team to refuse Putin’s demands.
The Russian leader not only wanted control of Ukraine but “he wants to redesign NATO to accommodate his revisionist ambitions,” Shaheen said, adding that any discussions about European security infrastructure should be a “nonstarter,” for the U.S. which “has benefited from the Alliance.”
Amid all of this, any substantial progress toward ending the war remains elusive.
The latest round of talks between the U.S., Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, last week produced no major breakthrough. Kushner said Washington was working toward what could be the largest prisoner swap of the war, while reporting that Russia had agreed to give Europe a seat at the table during the next round.
Russia hasn’t quite confirmed that, instead saying that it needs “to understand from the Europeans themselves” what they can “contribute to the peace process” before allowing them to join, as Putin’s spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters Monday.
There has been some internal wrangling among the European nations about who might represent them. Leaders have agreed on a team comprising the United Kingdom (which left the E.U. in 2020), France, Germany, Italy and Poland, alongside representatives of the European Commission and European Council. Kallas herself was left off the team.
“I don’t know who among the current leaders could be a sane dialogue partner,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov told the state-run news agency Tass on Monday.
He likened the chosen group of European countries to “the Quartet,” a satirical poem by Russian author Ivan Krylov. In it, a monkey, a donkey, a goat and a bear blame their failure to form a string

articles.title_orig: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
articles.title_zh: Google makes it easier to use Gemini without training AI on your data
articles.content_orig:
It can be hard to use Google products—or even the Internet itself—without coming into contact with Gemini AI. That is, of course, by design . The more you use Gemini, the more data Google collects to train and improve its generative AI chatbot. The options to limit training on your data have been scant, but Google is finally adding more controls to the Gemini app.
The change currently rolling out to Gemini will separate your chat history from training, which allows you to retain basic AI functionality without handing Google quite so much control over your data. Prior to this change, the only way to opt out of contributing your chat contents (including attachments) for training was to turn off your history. That made it impossible to go back and pick up a chat down the road.
As the new settings roll out, users will see separate toggles for model training and chat history. The history setting will continue to support an adjustable limit, but you will no longer have to change it to stop Google from training on your Gemini usage. Meanwhile, AI training will be an opt-out situation. You’ll need to find the toggle to block Google from using your chats for AI training. It’s under Activity in the Gemini settings. You can also access the menu from your Google account under Data and Privacy > My Activity > Other activity > Gemini Apps Activity.
Importantly, this only applies to future interactions with Gemini. If you have previously fed any data into Google’s AI, that’s already part of the training data. That can include your inputs, Gemini’s responses, uploaded files, tool calls, your location, and data from connected apps. Google says it may retain this data for up to three years to improve its models. The company has previously noted it attempts to filter personal information out of the Gemini activity history, but that isn’t a guarantee.
Regardless of your chosen activity settings, you can always manually remove anything you don’t want saved on the same page with the history and training toggles. However, reviewed chats that are already part of the training data won’t be retroactively deleted. Opting out of training doesn’t mean Google won’t have your data, either. Google may use this data in other ways for up to three years—it just won’t add it to AI-training data sets.
If you want to use Gemini and not retain any data, your options are actually a bit more limited now. Currently, if you disable history, Google still retains that data for 72 hours (and 24 hours for the user). Once the updated page is live, this duration will change to two months. So you can access that data for longer, but so can Google. The company says this is to “respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public.” Essentially, Google will be more able to identify nefarious AI usage even if someone disables history.
Even with the longer chat retention, the ability to control AI training is still a welcome privacy improvement. Google says the change is rolling out globally, but it may take a few weeks to show up for everyone.

articles.title_orig: Deutsche Bank Leak Exposes Epstein Payments—Democrats Could Hold It And Other Banks Accountable
articles.title_zh: Deutsche Bank Leak Exposes Epstein Payments—Democrats Could Hold It And Other Banks Accountable
articles.content_orig:
Deutsche Bank shares fell sharply in early trading on Tuesday after whistleblowers leaked about 15 million files from the German lender, with media reports revealing alleged historic failures across its risk management and financial crime controls.
These include suspicious payments linked to late financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, and accidental leaks of President Donald Trump 's tax statements.
The leaks contain board minutes, emails, internal investigations and other material that point to systemic failures across the Frankfurt-listed lender's business functions stretching back two decades.
Shares in Deutsche Bank were 4.7% lower by 9:20 a.m. E.T., having fallen more than 6% in early trade in Frankfurt.
Deutsche Bank processed $582 million in suspicious payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein, far more than previously known, the FT reported . Suspicious payments are not, by themselves, proof that every transaction was criminal.
The German lender also mistakenly leaked details of U.S. President Donald Trump's taxes in March 2017, during his first term in office, the FT said. The blunder — described by CEO Christian Sewing, who was then Deutsche's private banking head, as "an awful mistake" — was kept secret from the White House.
The wide-ranging investigation — which was led by a consortium of more than 200 journalists worldwide including the FT, Der Spiegel and Le Monde — also said Deutsche Bank had failed to offboard around 28,000 problematic investment bank clients who had been identified for removal by early 2018.
It also alleges that the bank concealed information around cost targets in 2021, when external monitors in New York reportedly warned that Deutsche's risk appetite was running ahead of controls.
The files also contain details of the bank's relationships with oligarchs and transactions that the investigation links to Russian money-laundering concerns. It was these ties that motivated whistleblowers to send the information to Indian journalist Josy Joseph and South African journalist Khadija Sharife.
The reports once again put Deutsche Bank's risk management practices and controls under the spotlight following years of regulatory scrutiny.
The bank — which has been raided multiple times by German officials this year — has, since 2012, paid out some 18.6 billion euros ($20.5 billion) in settlements over alleged market manipulation, money laundering, mis-selling and misrepresentation, among other things, the FT said.
In a statement, Deutsche Bank said the issues detailed in Tuesday's media reports go back many years.
"Where relevant, we reviewed these matters at the time and worked closely with regulators," the lender said.
The bank said it has undergone a "fundamental transformation" under CEO Christian Sewing, pointing to 7 billion euros of investment in its risk controls between 2019 and 2025.
"Deutsche Bank is a different bank today and remains focused on executing its strategy which has proven successful, as evidenced by record profits in 2025 as well as in recent quarters."
CNBC has reached out to BaFin, Germany's financial regulator, for comment.

articles.title_orig: 6-year-old girl dies in gene-editing trial, leading to scientist's firing, Chinese state media reports
articles.title_zh: 6-year-old girl dies in gene-editing trial, leading to scientist's firing, Chinese state media reports
articles.content_orig:
A Chinese scientist who concealed the death of a 6-year-old girl in a gene-editing trial has been fired following a government probe, according to state media.
The girl died last year after receiving experimental gene therapy to correct a non-life-threatening condition — which was not disclosed in published research, an investigation found in July.
Neuroscientist Zilong Qiu, the trial's lead researcher, had made no mention of the girl in a paper published in the prestigious journal Nature, according to the joint investigation by Science and Retraction Watch .
"According to official documents and accounts provided by the girl's parents, the hospital had allowed Qiu's experimental treatment to proceed under a regulatory provision that does not require approval from national regulators," Science reported in July. "After the child's death, the hospital paid a modest fine to a local health authority but Qiu was not publicly sanctioned."
Qiu was dismissed as deputy director of the Songjiang Research Institute affiliated with Shanghai Jiao Tong University, state broadcaster CCTV said Friday, citing a statement from Shanghai authorities.
The reported statement included only Qiu's surname, but referenced the Nature study published on Feb. 18.
Qiu was given a five-year suspension from participating in scientific projects and recorded in a database for "serious breaches of research integrity," the report said.
Another researcher on Qiu's team was fired and handed a five-year suspension, while several others with ties to the hospital where the trial took place were also punished.
The child who died had a rare neurodevelopmental condition called Snijders Blok-Campeau syndrome, according to the report.
The hospital's ethics committee had approved a gene-editing trial to treat the disorder in January 2025, the report said.
The committee terminated the study after the girl died in March due to complications from gene therapy.
Shanghai authorities found that Qiu's team failed to properly inform the hospital of possible safety issues from earlier tests on primates, according to the report.
AFP has reached out to Qiu for comment.
The July investigation by Science and Retraction Watch found that the girl's parents, who paid more than $800,000 to fund the experiment, were not adequately informed about the risks.
"Learning the reality of these missing safeguards has fundamentally changed how we now view the entire project," the girl's father, told Science . "We did not realize how unusual and dangerous many of the arrangements were."
The scandal is a blow to China's ambitions to rival the United States as a biotech power following the 2018 scandal around He Jiankui , a biophysicist who secretly produced gene-edited babies. He was later sentenced to three years in prison.
